activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
The bowl had survived sixty years of Sunday dinners, two transatlantic flights and a grandmother who stacked dishes like a woman daring the universe to try something. It did not survive Maria's first week as a counselor-in-training at Camp Wren, where she had set it on the windowsill of the craft cabin to remind herself of a kitchen four hundred miles away, and where Denis, reaching past it for the glitter glue, clipped it with his elbow and sent it to the floor in three clean pieces.

"Denis," Maria said, with the calm of someone deciding what kind of person she was going to be about this.

"I am already dead," Denis announced, lying down on the floor beside the shards in a display of solidarity that helped nobody. "Just bury me with it. Tell my mother I died doing something pointless."

Tianna crouched and touched the largest piece with one careful finger. "It's the blue one, isn't it. The one you said your grandma brought over on the boat." She looked up. "You showed it to me the first night. You said it was older than her."

Maria knelt and gathered the pieces into her palm. The break was sharp, decisive, almost elegant, though she did not want to admit that anything about this was elegant. She was aware of a small, petulant voice in her head insisting that Denis should suffer, that suffering would restore the bowl, which was obviously untrue and which she told, firmly, to be quiet.

"You're not throwing it out," Tianna said. It was not quite a question.

"Obviously not throwing it out."

"Okay, so." Tianna stood, dusted her knees, and gestured at the craft cabin around them, at the shelves of felt and popsicle sticks and the bin labeled MIXED: MISC. "So we fix it. This is literally the building where we fix things. There's a whole glue situation over there that portends great things."

The glue situation, however, was a lie. School glue would leave grey seams like scars. Superglue would work but hide the break entirely, and something in Maria bristled at that, at making sixty years and one afternoon of Denis pretend nothing had happened. She said as much at dinner, waving a fork for emphasis, and Denis said, "It's a bowl, not a diary," and Tianna said, "It's both, obviously, everything your grandma owns is both," and Maria conceded the point with a roll of eyes that meant she had already won.

That night she sat on the porch of Ms. Yamamoto's cabin, because Ms. Yamamoto ran the craft program and owned, according to Tianna, "actual tools, like an adult." Maria laid the three pieces on the steps between them.

Ms. Yamamoto turned them over without comment, then went inside and came back with a small tin and a paper packet that rattled.

"I won't do it for you," she said, which was not what Maria had been planning to ask, and therefore exactly what she'd been planning to ask. "My grandmother had a bowl like this. I broke it when I was eleven and she made me sit with it for a week before she'd teach me."

"Sit with it?"

"Decide what the break was going to mean. You can decide that. You can't decide that it didn't happen." Ms. Yamamoto opened the tin, showing a dark, viscous lacquer, and then the packet, which held a fine gold dust that caught the porch light and glittered like something expensive and slightly absurd. "You mix the lacquer with this, or dust it on while the seam's still wet. Gold powder. It's an old Japanese repair, called kintsugi. The crack becomes part of the history instead of something you hide."

"Gold," Maria said. "On my grandmother's everyday bowl."

"It was an everyday bowl," Ms. Yamamoto agreed, and there was something in her voice, some raised eyebrow buried in it, that Maria chose to hear as permission.

The next two evenings she worked at the picnic table behind the craft cabin while Tianna read aloud from a trashy novel and Denis, still performing his guilt like community theater, kept arriving with offerings: a lemonade, a bag of chips, once a single carnation he had definitely picked from the flagpole garden. Maria declared a general amnesty for elbows, the window ledge, and all glitter-related crimes, and Denis bowed so deeply he knocked over the lemonade, which everyone agreed was extremely on brand.

The lacquer went on with a toothpick, slower than Maria expected, and the first seam came out crooked. She scraped it, waited, tried again. Tianna leaned over her shoulder and said, "You're not going to sand that flat, are you," in the tone of someone already knowing, and Maria said no, she was not going to sand it flat, and gold dust settled into the wet seam and made the crooked line look deliberate, which it was not, and which she decided not to explain to anyone.

She turned the finished bowl in her hands in the last light. The gold ran across the blue like a river on a map, crooked, bright, permanent, wrong and right at once. She did not know whether her grandmother would see a repair or a ruin, whether she'd laugh or go quiet the way she did at the mention of the boat, and Maria held both possibilities easily, the way the bowl now held its whole history in a visible line.

Denis leaned in beside her, examining it.

"So it's better now," he said.

"It's more now," Maria said, and set it on the window ledge, crooked seam facing the lake.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging 'ibid.' in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title.
story:
The red ink sat at the bottom of page four like a burn. Mr. Gill, who was technically a neighbour but had agreed to read the draft because he had once taught history, had circled the word "Ibid." three times and written "outdated" in the margin. William had copied the citation style from his grandfather's style guide, a squat green book with a cracked spine that lived on the shelf between the atlas and the fishing manuals, and it had seemed unimpeachable. It was a book, printed and bound, older than William's father. Now it seemed the book had quietly gone wrong somewhere without telling anyone.

The paper was due Thursday. It was Monday evening, and the crepuscular light through the library's tall windows had gone violet and then grey, and the fluorescent ceiling panels were taking over, giving everything a flat, aquarium calm. William spread the marked draft across the table and, beside it, the green guide, and stared at them as though the two documents might be encouraged to argue directly with each other.

Kylan arrived first, sliding into the opposite chair with his backpack still on one shoulder. "You texted me a photo of the word 'ibid.' with eleven question marks," he said. "So I came."

"It's Latin," William said. "It means the same source as before. My grandfather used it his whole career. Mr. Gill says it's outdated, but he didn't say what to do instead."

Flora came next, carrying two granola bars and a mug that said WORLD'S ADEQUATE LIBRARIAN, which she set down with ceremony. "That's the librarian's mug," William said. "You can't just take the librarian's mug." Flora said she had traded for it, and when William asked what the remuneration had been, she said one unexpired cough drop, and the matter was settled.

They worked. Kylan pulled the reference copies, the newer manuals that the library kept behind the desk because people apparently stole citation guides, a fact William found almost touching. Flora opened her laptop and typed with the flat efficiency she saved for things she considered beneath effort. William himself sat with the stack of note cards his grandfather had taught him to make, one fact per card, source in the corner, and felt the two systems, the cards and the screens, regarding each other across the table like rival delegations.

It was Flora who found it, or rather Flora who read aloud the sentence William had been circling toward without recognizing. "The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style," she read, "published in 2017, started discouraging 'ibid.'" She scrolled. "In favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title." She looked up. "So you don't use 'ibid.' anymore. You just say the author's name again and a short version of the title."

William felt something loosen in his chest, though he noticed he did not feel vindicated, exactly, and he did not feel defeated either. His grandfather had not been wrong. He had been right for a book published before William was born, and then the world had shifted under the book, gently, without ceremony. The guide itself was not a fraud. It was a photograph of a moment that had passed.

He tested it. In the third footnote he wrote the author's name and a shortened title where "Ibid." had been, and the fourth, and the fifth, and the rhythm of it was different, less elegant in a way, more repetitive, but clearer too, a stranger could read any single footnote and know where it came from without hunting backwards through the page. He worked through the draft with a pen, and Kylan checked the bibliography against the notes, and Flora, unsolicited, reformatted the whole thing into hanging indents and refused to explain what a hanging indent was, only pointing.

Mr. Gill came by at closing, moving from table to table with the unhurried gait of a man who had spent forty years underwriting other people's curiosity, buying books and shelving them and trusting that somebody would eventually come. He paused at William's table. He looked at the corrected footnotes for a long moment, long enough that William began to worry there was a second thing wrong.

"Better," he said finally. "Though your grandfather wasn't a fool. Styles change. The people who made them don't."

William said he had started to think that himself. He said it carefully, because it was only half worked out. He still didn't know whether the new way was better or merely newer, whether clarity was worth the ugliness of repetition, whether his grandfather, who had believed in economy, would have made the change or dug in. He said some of this out loud, and Mr. Gill said nothing, only tapped the green guide once with two fingers, the way you'd acknowledge an opponent in a match, and moved on toward the desk.

The lights dimmed in stages, the way they did, a polite warning rather than an eviction. Flora returned the mug. Kylan carried the reference manuals back while William gathered his cards, and the cards went into his pocket instead of the bin, because they were his grandfather's system and his grandfather's habit and he was not prepared to decide anything final about them at seventeen, at a library table, on a Monday.

Outside, the streetlights had come on. William zipped his bag over the corrected draft, and Kylan, walking backward toward the bus stop, called out, "So what do I tell my dad when he says 'ibid.' at dinner?"

"Tell him the 17th edition happened," William said. "Tell him it's 2017 somewhere in Chicago, and we're all just catching up." Then he slung the bag over his shoulder and crossed the street against the last of the violet light.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The 2018 Gender Shades study by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru found commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women but under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men.
story:
The library's new self-checkout kiosk had been rejecting Aydin's face for the third morning in a row, and Brody had begun timing it. Eleven seconds, then a yellow banner: patron not recognized. When Christian stepped up beside him, the screen unlocked in under a second, before he had even finished raising his student card.

"It doesn't like me," Aydin said, without much inflection, the way he said most things. He tapped the manual override and held his books against the scanner one at a time.

Brody watched the screen dim back to its welcome message, a stock photo of a smiling woman who was neither of them. He wondered what the camera was actually looking for, whether it measured jawlines or the space between the eyes, and whether whatever it measured could simply forget people. "It's not liking," he said. "It's math. Which is maybe worse, because math is supposed to be neutral."

They claimed the table by the window, the one with the wobble that Mr. Gauthier kept meaning to fix. Aydin spread out his notes for the robotics elective they all took, and Christian, ebullient as always after acing a quiz he hadn't studied for, started narrating the kiosk's failures to anyone who would listen. "It knows me instantly," he said. "I walk past it and it practically bows."

That was when Brody remembered the research he'd found two weeks earlier, hunched over the same table at midnight, hunting for a citation on algorithmic accountability. He'd opened a paper from 2018 by Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru called the Gender Shades study, and the numbers had stopped him cold: commercial facial analysis systems had error rates up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women, and under 1 percent for lighter-skinned men. He'd read the figure twice, then a third time, because the gap seemed too large to be an accident and too specific to be a lie. He hadn't printed it, hadn't saved it, and now he couldn't remember whether he'd closed the tab out of laziness or out of something closer to embarrassment, as if the numbers were a thing he'd overheard through a wall.

He pulled it up again on the library computer, the slow one near the reference desk whose fan sounded like a small animal trapped under the floor. "Here," he said, turning the screen toward Aydin. "Two thousand eighteen. Up to 34.7 percent error for darker-skinned women. Under one percent for lighter-skinned men."

Aydin read it with his chin propped on his fist. Christian leaned in over his shoulder, and for once he didn't say anything clever. "So it's not broken," Aydin said finally. "It's working the way it was built."

"That's the part I can't stop chewing on," Brody said. "Nobody at the kiosk company sat in a room and decided to fail you specifically. But somebody chose the training data, or didn't check it, and the choice ossified into a system that treats the failure as Aydin's problem. Every morning you get the yellow banner and everyone pretends it's a glitch." He tapped the margin of his notes. "In robotics Mr. Gauthier keeps saying the machine is only as good as what we feed it. I used to think that was about batteries."

Aydin pulled out his phone and held it up, angling it toward the kiosk across the room where a younger girl was being waved through by the same camera that had stalled him. "So what do we do with this? File a complaint? Stand here being evidence?"

The question sat between them for a moment, and Brody let it, because he didn't have a position yet, only two competing instincts: that pointing at the machine was useless unless you pointed at the hands that built it, and that the girl would keep walking through while Aydin kept tapping override whether or not anyone pointed at anything. Maybe both were true at once. "We could measure it," he said slowly, the idea arriving as he said it. "Ten people, ten tries each, actual stopwatch times. Bring the numbers to Mr. Gauthier and let him decide whether the library keeps paying for it."

Aydin looked at him, then at the kiosk, then began stacking his books. "Go get the stopwatch on your phone," he said. "I'll go stand in front of it again."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
Naomi had promised Ms. Otieno her summary by first period, which meant she had roughly eleven hours to read a Spanish news article, understand it, and say it back aloud without her voice doing that wobbling thing it did on the word "internacional." The article was short, three paragraphs, printed off at the library because her mother had claimed the family laptop for a spreadsheet of querulous proportions, a budget document that muttered at her from across the kitchen table. So Naomi sat at the counter with a pencil, a paper dictionary, and her phone propped against the sugar bowl, Sloan's face filling the screen.

"Read me the first line," Sloan said. Sloan had done this last semester, in French, and now behaved like a customs official at the border of languages. "Whole line. No stopping in the middle to panic."

Naomi read. Her pronunciation was mostly guesswork, and the guessing showed. Somewhere around the second sentence she lost the thread entirely and improvised a summary instead: "It's about, um, a factory. In Mexico? Or maybe France. A factory somewhere doing something with water."

Sloan's silence had a specific texture to it, the texture of a person deciding not to laugh. "France. Your article is in Spanish and you think it's about France."

"Mexico, then. Somewhere hot."

"You skipped the beginning," Sloan said. "Go back. Before the first sentence. There's a thing there."

Naomi turned back to the top of the page, feeling faintly cheated, as though the article had been hiding evidence. Before the first sentence sat a small block of caps: a city name, then a date. She had glided straight over it, eyes already hungry for verbs. "Lima," she said slowly. "It says Lima."

"There you go. It's called a dateline. It's the city where the story was reported." Sloan leaned closer to the camera, nearly becoming a nostril. "My whole class got a lecture about it after Maxx told the teacher his French article happened in Canada and it was actually Senegal. Maxx tried to expostulate. He stood up and said, 'But the sentence doesn't say where it is,' and Ms. Otieno said, 'The dateline says where it is, Maxx,' and he sat down like a folding chair."

Naomi wrote LIMA at the top of her notes and underlined it twice, then once more for luck. It changed the whole shape of the article, suddenly. Not a generic factory doing something with water but a specific one, in a specific city, and the second paragraph's complaint about the river made a new kind of sense. She looked up the unfamiliar words one by one, apportioning her remaining evening in a way she pretended was strategic: twenty minutes for vocabulary, ten for reading aloud to the microwave, and the last stretch for building the summary itself. The apportionment collapsed immediately, as all such plans did, when the dictionary took fourteen minutes on a single verb.

"Say the summary to me," Sloan said. "Pretend I'm Ms. Otieno. Be terrified."

Naomi cleared her throat. "The article, reported from Lima, is about a factory that may have polluted a river. The people who live near it say the water changed color. The company says it followed the rules. The government has not decided yet."

"That was," Sloan said, "actually good. Weirdly good. Now say it again but like a person and not a hostage."

They ran it four more times. By the third, Naomi could feel where her voice would wobble and could steer around it, and by the fourth she had smuggled in a small joke about the company's lawyer that made Sloan snort tea onto their own desk, which Sloan reported as her proudest achievement of the week. On the fifth pass Naomi stalled on a word, and instead of freezing she circled it, said "the, uh, the river part," and kept going, which Sloan declared the single most important skill of oral summarizing, more important even than knowing the words.

Her mother looked up from the spreadsheet long enough to say that if Naomi was going to perform at the counter all night, she should at least refill the kettle. Naomi filled it, set it on, and while it heated she read the article one final time, straight through, dateline first, and was surprised to find she barely stumbled at all.

At eleven her phone buzzed. Sloan had sent a photo of Maxx's forehead, presumably the rest of him somewhere below, with the caption: he says good luck and also what's a dateline.

Naomi typed back: city where the story was reported, before the first sentence, and added, tell him Canada misses him. Then she flipped her notes face down, looked at the ceiling, and gave the summary once more, from memory, all the way to the end. "The government," she said to the empty kitchen, "has not decided yet," and the kettle, right on cue, began to whistle.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: After a LEFT JOIN, COUNT of an orders column gives 0 for customers without orders, but COUNT(*) gives 1, because it counts the NULL-filled row.
story:
The shop smelled of solder and orange cleaner, and behind the counter Ms. Gallagher kept a battered laptop that held every customer she had served since the place opened. Alexis had started helping there on Saturdays in June, mostly entering names and phone numbers into a spreadsheet, until Ms. Gallagher admitted that the spreadsheet had become three spreadsheets, then a database, then a mess.

"Half these people never came back," Ms. Gallagher said one afternoon, sliding a mug of tea across the counter. "I'd like to know which half. Can you write me one of your queries?"

Alexis had finished an online course in June, the kind that gave a certificate as a PDF. She knew SELECT and WHERE and a little of JOIN. She sat on the stool behind the register and opened the laptop. The customers table had three hundred rows. The orders table, which tracked every screen replacement and battery swap, had over a thousand.

Jiya came in at four with a cracked tablet, and while Ms. Gallagher was in the back looking for a part, Jiya leaned over Alexis's shoulder. "What are you doing?"

"Trying to find customers who never ordered anything," Alexis said. She typed the join, LEFT JOIN she remembered, because a lecture had said it kept every row from the first table even when nothing matched. She counted the results, grouped by customer, and filtered for anything with a count of zero.

The screen came back empty.

"That can't be right," Jiya said. "The indigent guy who comes in for free chargers, the one Ms. Gallagher never charges. He's been in here twice and never ordered a thing."

Alexis ran a plain count of the results. Three hundred customers, every one of them with a count of at least one. "According to this, everybody ordered something."

"Then it's wrong."

"It's wrong or I'm wrong." Alexis scrolled the output. There was the charger man, his row sitting alone with no order beside it, blank cells where the order number should have been. And there, in her count column, a one. She looked at it for a long moment. The row existed, even if the order in it was empty. She had used COUNT(*), the star, the count of everything, and it had counted the blank row itself.

She changed one character. Instead of counting everything, she counted the order number column, and ran it again. The charger man now showed a zero. So did forty-one others, names she recognized and names she didn't, people who had walked in once for advice or a price quote and never come back.

"There," she said.

Jiya frowned at the screen. "So the star counts the blank row, and counting the column doesn't."

"That's what it did." Alexis wrote both versions down in her notebook, one above the other, and underlined the difference. It was strange to her that a query could tell the truth and lie at once, depending on which truth you asked for. Whether a person had a row, and whether a person had an order, were not the same question, and she had asked the first one while believing she asked the second.

Ms. Gallagher came out from the back with a tablet battery in her hand. "Did you get my list?"

"I got a list." Alexis turned the laptop toward her. "Forty-two customers who never ordered anything. But I'd check it against the paper invoices before you trust it. The data in the orders table is only as good as what got typed in."

Ms. Gallagher put on her glasses and scrolled slowly. "Ramirez. He brought in his daughter's phone, I fixed it, he paid cash. That never went in the system." She tapped the screen. "So this says he ordered nothing, and that's false."

"Then the query is right and the data is wrong," Alexis said. She was careful to say it that way, because she had learned the week before not to promise more than the machine could deliver. "The join finds who's missing from orders. It can't tell you why they're missing."

Jiya had claimed a chair by the window and was picking at the edge of her tablet bag. "So you can't actually answer her question."

"I can answer it if the records are complete. I can't fix the records from here." Alexis looked at the two lists side by side, the one where everyone counted and the one where forty-two people didn't, and neither one was the whole truth by itself. She thought of her mother, who did the books for a bakery and always said the software was only as honest as the person holding the receipt.

Ms. Gallagher pulled a stool up to the counter. "The paper invoices are in the cabinet under the register. Sorted by month, not by name, I'm afraid."

"That's fine," Alexis said. "We'll go through them and fix the table, and then I'll run it again." She copied her query to a file and named it customers_with_no_orders_v2. "Jiya, you're staying."

Jiya sighed and dragged her chair over to the cabinet. Ms. Gallagher unlocked it, and the three of them began pulling out folders, thick with receipts, the oldest ones soft and faded at the edges.

"Start with June," Ms. Gallagher said, laying the first folder open on the glass counter.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, published in 1790, condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, and set the conservative view that historians after 1800 argued with.
story:
Landon spread seven library books across the kitchen table, three of them still damp from his backpack, and discovered that his laptop had died in the night, which meant his outline existed only in the cloud, which meant his outline existed nowhere. The essay was due Thursday. Ms. Chukwu had set the question on a single photocopied page, now pinned under a fruit bowl: "How have historians' views of the French Revolution changed since 1800?" He had read that sentence perhaps forty times, and each time it seemed to be about a different revolution, one that had happened in a country called Historiography.

His mother slid a mug of tea onto the only clear patch of table. "You look like a man being audited," she said.

"I'm being audited by two hundred years of French scholars. They all hate each other." He picked up the thickest book, a survey from 1967 whose author called an earlier generation "sentimental," and put it down again. "I don't even know where to start. Everyone starts somewhere different. It's like a relay race where the runners are arguing about who dropped the baton in 1793."

His mother demurred, in her way, which was to say "hmm" and leave the room. He texted Yara instead, because Yara had finished her essay on Sunday, which was a fact she had mentioned four times.

Yara replied within a minute, in the long bursts she used when she was avoiding her own homework. "start with burke," she wrote. "everyone starts with burke. he's basically patient zero." Then: "my guy, the conservative view starts with him, the historians after 1800 are all just yelling at him or yelling at people who yelled at him." Then a string of small waving ghosts, her signature signoff.

Landon typed "burke the MP? didn't he write before 1800" and got back "1790. reflections on the revolution in france. it condemned the whole thing for destroying tradition. yes before 1800, that's the point, you need the before to see the after." He sat with that. The prompt said since 1800, and Burke was 1790, so for an hour he had been treating the man as off-limits, a trespasser behind the historical fence. But Yara's way of putting it had turned the fence into a doorway. If you wanted to know what historians after 1800 were arguing with, you needed the thing they were arguing with to be standing there, in print, being wrong at them.

Noam arrived at six with a bag of clementines and no invitation, as usual. He sat down, peeled a clementine in one unbroken spiral, which was his only documented talent, and read the photocopied prompt upside down. "So you're writing about writers writing about a revolution," he said. "That's, like, three mirrors deep. Do you ever get to the actual guillotine?"

"Sometimes. Mostly you get the apportionment of blame. Who gets how much." Landon tapped the 1967 survey. "This guy gives the Jacobins forty percent and circumstance sixty. The guy before him gives circumstance nothing. There's a whole literature just on the math."

"That's bleak. I'd rather write about volcanoes." Noam flicked a segment of clementine at him. "Fine, be sectarian about your dead Frenchmen. I'm eating your mother's biscuits."

Landon built the essay the way Yara's texts suggested: Burke in the first paragraph, not as an event but as a fixed point. Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790, the book that condemned the Revolution for destroying tradition, and the position that later historians pushed against. Then the pushing. A liberal historian who apologized for the Terror, then a Marxist who treated the whole thing as a class project with casualties, then a revisionist in the 1950s who dismantled the class story, then the social historians who reassembled it with different parts. Each one defined itself against something, and often the something was Burke's ghost, still presiding, still disliked. By ten o'clock Landon had four pages and a plate of clementine peels.

The uncertainty arrived with the conclusion. He wanted to say that historiography was progress, that each generation got closer to the truth of 1789, but the books wouldn't quite let him; the revisionists had dismantled a story that had been, in its own era, genuinely persuasive, and the post-revisionists had restored parts of it, and the pattern looked less like ascent than like weather. He wrote a sentence claiming that each school reflected its own century more than the eighteenth, then deleted it because it sounded like a fortune cookie, then wrote a softer version and deleted that too. In the end he left a paragraph that said the argument had a shape he could describe but not a destination he could name, which felt like admitting a crime, and he underlined it and wrote "keep? or cowardly?" in the margin.

Ms. Chukwu's reply came the next morning, after he'd emailed her the draft at an hour he would not confess to. "Good," she wrote. "The Burke paragraph does real work. The last paragraph stays honest without collapsing into mush. One caution: don't apologize for uncertainty. Make the reader sit in it." Then a second message, three minutes later: "Also, tell Noam the clementine spiral is showing up in other students' margins and I know exactly who to blame."

Landon printed the draft, and the pages came out warm, and he carried them to the kitchen table where the seven library books still lay open like patient dogs. He set the stack of essays on top of Burke's successors, weighed down at last, and texted Yara a single ghost.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In a time signature, the top number gives the number of beats in each bar and the bottom number gives the note value that gets one beat, so 4/4 means four quarter-note beats.
story:
The music room smelled of valve oil and old radiator dust, and Autumn had claimed the piano bench by the window because the light there made the staff paper easier to read. The assignment on the board read sixteen bars, chord changes, standard notation, due Friday, and Mr. Halvorsen had underlined notation twice, which everyone understood to mean he was tired of receiving voice memos. She had a melody in her head. The problem was that it would not sit still long enough to be written down.

"You're humming again," said Wayne, dropping into the chair beside her with his own paper, which he had covered in a scrawl of notes. "Every time you hum, my bars go wrong."

"Your bars were wrong before I hummed." She leaned over and counted his first line, tapping her pencil under each note head. One, two, three, four, five. She counted the second bar. Five again. "Wayne. Some of these bars have five beats in them."

He looked at the page as though it had betrayed him personally. "So what time signature is it in?"

Aydin, who was dismantling a clarinet reed two chairs down for no reason anyone had ever established, said without looking up, "It's not in one yet. That's the whole point of writing it down. The top number tells you how many beats in each bar, and the bottom number tells you which note gets one beat. So 4/4 means four quarter-note beats." He held the reed up to the light. "Five beats a bar would be 5/4, if you meant it. Did you mean it?"

"I meant music," Wayne said with dignity.

Autumn laughed, and then stopped laughing, because something in her own head had shifted. She had been trying to force her melody into four neat beats, like packing a suitcase that was slightly too small, sitting on the lid. Maybe the melody was not the problem. Maybe the box was. She pulled a fresh sheet toward her and drew bar lines where the melody actually breathed, and when she counted, three of the bars held five quarter-note beats, and it felt less like an error and more like the tune had been waiting for someone to give it permission.

"It's harder than it looks," she admitted. "Changing the metre halfway. My hands want to keep the old pattern." She played it through, clumsy, stopping twice. The five-beat bars staggered and then found a gait of their own, like a person walking on a slightly uneven sidewalk who decides to enjoy it.

"You realize," Wayne said, watching her pencilling chords above the staff, "that you're now doing more work than the assignment requires, voluntarily, on a Wednesday." He was not wrong, and she told him so, and he prevaricated for a while about how he had definitely been about to try 5/4 himself, which fooled no one, least of all Aydin, who snorted into the bell of his clarinet. Autumn thought that the pragmatics of the room were simple: Wayne needed a deadline, Aydin needed an audience, and she needed exactly this, a bench, a window, and two people loud enough to drown out her own second-guessing.

Mr. Halvorsen came in mid-afternoon to collect the metronomes and paused behind her, long enough that she felt the shadow fall across the page. "Play the fifth bar again," he said. She did. He was quiet a moment. "That turn at the end. Where did you find it?"

"I didn't find it. I made it up this morning."

He sat down at the second piano, the one with the chipped D, and played her phrase, then played something that followed from it, and she recognized it with a small cold shock. It was the hymn her grandmother used to hum while washing dishes, the one Autumn had assumed she'd forgotten along with most of the rest of that year. "You didn't make it up," Mr. Halvorsen said, not unkindly. "You remembered it. Composers have been doing this for centuries. Brahms was not above it."

"So it's not mine," she said, and the sentence landed heavier than she expected, like finding out a gift she'd treasured had been regifted to her first.

"The five-beat bars are yours. The chord under that F-sharp is definitely yours, and it's a brave one. The rest you borrowed from a woman who lent it to you for free." He stood, gathered the last metronome under his arm, and paused at the door. "You could ask her about it, you know. She might tell you where she got it."

The room went quiet except for Aydin's reed, ticking softly against the table. Autumn looked at her sixteen bars, at the borrowed phrase wearing her chords like a new coat, and felt simultaneously rich and destitute, owner of nothing and of more than she'd had at breakfast. She picked up her pencil and, under the title she hadn't known she was going to write, printed For my grandmother, and after a moment added, in smaller letters, who is still alive, and I should call her.

"Friday," Wayne reminded her, holding up his paper, which now had 5/4 pencilled angrily across the top. "We're both doomed."

"Only you," Aydin said. "I'm percussion. I just hit things."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO credit score, making up about 35 percent of it for the general population.
story:
The line at the bank moved slowly, and Jordyn counted the tiles on the floor twice before Muhammad nudged her. "You're grinding your teeth," he said. She unclenched her jaw and looked at the folder in her lap, the one holding her acceptance letter, her budget on graph paper, and the deposit slip for the money she'd saved over two summers of pushing bagels across a counter.

She needed a small loan, twelve hundred dollars, to cover the housing deposit for the dorm her financial aid didn't reach. Her mother had said no flatly, standing at the sink with her back turned, and Jordyn had spent the drive downtown trying to decide whether that had been cruelty or honesty.

There was one thing she hadn't told Muhammad. In the spring she'd forgotten a phone bill, forty dollars, for six weeks, while her hours got cut and her attention went to exams and her grandmother's hospital visits. She'd paid it the day the third notice came, but something about it had been sitting under her ribs since, the way a library fine sits small and wrong until you walk past the desk.

"Next," the teller called, and Ms. Gill, the loan officer whose desk sat behind a low partition, waved them over. She had reading glasses on a chain and a legal thriller lying facedown beside her keyboard, and she asked Jordyn to sit before she'd finished saying hello.

"Twelve hundred, repaid over a year," Jordyn said. "I work twenty-five hours a week. I have nine hundred saved already." She slid the graph paper across. Ms. Gill looked at it longer than Jordyn expected, tapping one column with her pen, and then pulled up the screen.

"Your score," Ms. Gill said, and paused. "It's not what I'd guess from this budget."

Jordyn's hands went cold on the armrests. "The phone bill," she said. "I paid it. Six weeks late, but I paid it, in full."

Ms. Gill turned the monitor so Jordyn could see it. "Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO score," she said. "For the general population it's about thirty-five percent." She said it the way she'd say a recipe, flat and quick, then pointed at the number on screen. "One late payment didn't ruin you. But you should know what you're working with."

Muhammad leaned over Jordyn's shoulder. "Thirty-five percent," he repeated. "For everybody?"

"For the general population," Ms. Gill said, and took her glasses off. "And the rest of the file looks thin. Short history, few accounts. You're young. That's not a crime, it's just a fact."

"So I can't get the loan," Jordyn said.

"I didn't say that." Ms. Gill clicked through a screen. "I can approve it. But the rate you're offered depends on that score, and interest means you'll pay back more than twelve hundred over time, more per month than the number on your nice graph paper there. Borrowed money costs more the longer you carry it." She wrote a figure on a sticky note and turned it around. Jordyn looked at it and felt the distance between the number and her budget the way you feel a step that isn't where your foot expected it.

"Or," Ms. Gill said, "you put the nine hundred in a savings account here instead of lending it to your sock drawer, and interest works the other way. Savings grow over time. Slowly, at your balance, honestly. But it goes in your direction instead of mine." She said it without a smile, which somehow made it easier to hear.

Jordyn sat with both options like two weights in her hands. Her mother's refusal had felt like a door slamming, but standing here it was more like a mirror, showing her the same arithmetic from a colder angle. Maybe she could pay the deposit in installments directly to the university and skip the loan entirely, though that meant asking the housing office for something not promised. Maybe she took the loan at the worse rate and let twelve on-time payments start building the history she didn't have, which felt like paying tuition twice. She didn't know which was the smarter version of stubborn, and she was tired of pretending she did.

"If I take it," she said slowly, "and I never miss a payment, does the score come back up?"

"It can," Ms. Gill said. "I'm not going to promise you a number. But nothing exonerates a file like time and clean payments." She capped her pen. "Decision's yours. I need an answer before my two o'clock, and before your friend there reads the rest of my novel." Muhammad was holding up the legal thriller, reading the back cover. "The subpoena twist is scathing," he said. "The blurb calls it scathing."

"It is," Ms. Gill said, taking it from him.

Jordyn pulled the deposit slip out of the folder and set it on the desk beside the sticky note, then looked up at the clock over the teller line. "Savings account first," she said. "Then let me make one phone call before I sign anything." She reached across the desk for Ms. Gill's pen.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Behavioral interview questions, such as 'Tell me about a time when...', are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior.
story:
Nicholas arrived at Simona's party holding his interview outfit in a garment bag, which was, everyone agreed, the funniest thing any guest had brought. The bag hung from the closet door like a ghost of Monday, because on Monday at four he would sit across from the manager of Alder Books and try to convince her he deserved the part-time opening, and he had never in his life convinced anyone of anything in an interview, having never had one.

"You brought the tie," Alessia said, delighted, dangling it by its narrow end. "You brought the tie to a birthday."

"It's a rehearsal tie," Nicholas said. "It's load-bearing."

Ms. Lin, who lived next door to Simona and had come over with a bowl of something she called "autochthonous to my grandmother's village, don't ask which village," overheard this and set the bowl down with the authority of a woman who had hired and fired perhaps forty people in her years managing a hotel. She had opinions. Simona's mother had warned them all about this at the door, smiling.

Twenty minutes later the party had reorganized itself without anyone planning to. The cake was still in its box, the music had been lowered in deference to what Alessia was calling "the tribunal," and Nicholas sat on the far end of the couch with his hands on his knees while Ms. Lin took the armchair like a bench. Simona perched on the arm beside him, whispering that he should stop looking at the floor as though the answer were written there.

"Tell me about a time," Ms. Lin began, "when you had to solve a problem as part of a team."

Nicholas looked at the floor. "I don't have any times," he said. "I've never had a job. I have nothing to tell you about."

"That," said Ms. Lin, "is the single most wrong thing you have said so far, and you've said several wrong things."

From the kitchen doorway, Simona watched Nicholas's shoulders climb toward his ears and felt a familiar, almost fraternal impatience. She had watched him do this in seminar all spring: receive a fair question, decide it was an ambush, and surrender before anyone had attacked. She also knew something he seemed to have forgotten, which was that he had once spent an entire weekend building a spreadsheet to figure out which of the school's vending machines actually restocked on schedule, and had then, with two other students, presented the data to the vice principal so convincingly that the contract got reviewed. She had been one of the two other students. She crossed the room and stood behind the couch like a witness taking the stand.

"He has a time," she announced. "The vending machine thing. Tell her."

"Tell me about the vending machine thing," Ms. Lin repeated, patient as tide.

Nicholas exhaled and began, haltingly, and then less haltingly, describing the project: the weeks of tallying, the disagreement about method, the moment his partner wanted to quit and he had, according to three people present and one of them currently eating cake in the kitchen, "recalibrated the whole approach, basically overnight." When he finished, his eyes had actually stayed on Ms. Lin's face for the entire last minute, which Alessia confirmed later by timing it on her phone.

"Better," Ms. Lin said. "Now understand what I was doing to you. Those are behavioral interview questions. The 'tell me about a time' ones. The whole idea behind them is that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior." She folded her hands. "So the questions aren't about your job history. They never were. They're about you, and you have been you for eighteen years, which is plenty of material."

Nicholas sat with that, turning it over the way he turned over a problem in a margin. It struck him as both reassuring and slightly sinister: the idea that Monday's questions were less about what he could do than about what he had already, unknowingly, filed away as evidence. It suggested a kind of teleology running backward through his life, every group project and abandoned hobby waiting to be repurposed as proof of competence, as though he had been accumulating a resume since childhood without being consulted. On the other hand, he had also once left a full trash bag on a bus, and he preferred not to think about what that predicted.

"Okay," he said slowly, "but what if they ask about a time I failed? Because there's the bus thing, and also the semester of Latin."

"Then you tell them the Latin," Ms. Lin said, "and you tell them what you did after."

"You mean like, grew as a person?"

"I mean like facts. What did you actually do."

"Tutoring," Nicholas admitted. "Tuesdays. It was fine."

Alessia raised her plastic cup. "To Tuesdays," she said. "To the tribunal. To the autochthonous bowl, which I have now eaten half of."

They cut the cake after that, and the interview receded into the noise of the party, resurfacing only when Simona dragged him to the hallway mirror and made him practice the eye contact until he laughed, which she claimed also counted as practice, since laughing people look directly at things.

On Monday at 3:52, Nicholas stood outside Alder Books with the rehearsal tie knotted slightly too tightly, watching through the window as the manager moved a display of field guides. He rolled his shoulders back, thought briefly of vending machines and Tuesdays and the strange arithmetic by which his past would now be read as his future, and pushed open the door.

"Nicholas," he said, extending his hand. "I'm the four o'clock."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The newspaper was free at the café door, and Simon's uncle had told him that if he wanted the language to stick, he should read one short article a day and say it back to someone. So Simon took the paper to the corner table, ordered a coffee he could not pronounce correctly, and unfolded the front page over the small marble table. The article he chose was maybe two hundred words, something about a river festival in the next town, and his task, assigned by himself that morning, was to read it and then summarise it aloud to his cousin's friend Amelia, who was meeting him at three.

The trouble was that he read the way he had been taught in school: left to right, word by word, stopping at every unfamiliar verb the way you stop at every stone in a badly paved street. After twenty minutes he had reached the third paragraph and understood perhaps half of it, and when he looked up, Amelia was already standing at the door, waving.

"You look like a lawyer preparing to litigate a parking ticket," she said, dropping into the other chair. "What are you doing to that poor newspaper?"

"Reading it." He turned the page toward her. "I have to summarise it out loud to you. That was the deal. But I keep getting stuck on words I don't need."

She pulled the paper across the table and glanced down it. "Do you need all of it, or do you just need to know what happened?"

"The general idea. The whole thing, in my own words."

Amelia tapped the column with two fingers. "At school they made us learn two different things, and everybody mixed them up. Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea. Scanning means searching for one specific detail, like a name or a number."

"Those sound the same."

"They're not. Watch." She took a pen from her bag, circled a word near the bottom of the article, and slid the paper back. "What's the date of the festival?"

Simon bent over the page and began at the top again, crawling line by line, mouthing the words. Amelia said nothing, but she drank her coffee in a way that made the silence conspicuous. When he finally found the date, four lines from the end, he sat back.

"That took me a minute."

"You read the whole article to find one number." She said it without cruelty, more like she was noticing the weather. "Scanning would be letting your eyes jump around until a number-shaped thing shows up. That's all. Ten seconds."

Simon looked at the page again, this time letting his eyes move the way she described, not gathering but hunting, and the date seemed almost to leap out, obvious and slightly insulted at having been missed. It was strange to think that the same page could be read in such different ways, that the text was not just one thing but depended on what you wanted from it. He wondered whether he had ever actually been taught this, or whether school had only ever rewarded him for being slow and complete.

"Okay," he said. "So skimming is what I need for the summary. Fast, general." He laid the paper flat and tried it, running his eyes down the paragraphs without stopping, refusing the unfamiliar words like a man declining every invitation at a party. It felt dishonest at first, reading without understanding every piece, and then it felt like something else: a kind of mercurial attention that jumped and returned, jumped and returned, and somehow carried more back each time than his old plodding method had.

"Now tell me," Amelia said.

He spoke haltingly, in the new language, his summary. The town on the river would hold its festival, there would be boats, the mayor had said something about the water being cleaner than in past years, and the date was the one he had found. It was a rough encapsulation of the article, imperfect, and he could hear the gaps where whole clauses had slipped past him. "I missed whatever that man said in the middle," he admitted. "The fisherman, I think."

"The fisherman said the herons came back."

"Herons." He wrote the word on the margin of the paper. "I would have found that eventually. Word by word."

"Yes, but then you'd have nothing else done today." Amelia folded the newspaper in half and pushed her empty cup aside. "So which way is better, do you think? Yours or the fast one?"

Simon considered the question honestly, because he suspected the honest answer was neither. Word by word gave him depth but cost him hours; skimming gave him the shape of things but left holes where herons should be. Maybe, he thought, you chose the tool for what you needed, and maybe what he needed would keep changing. "I don't know yet," he said. "Ask me again in a month."

"Fine. Same table, same coffee, one article." She stood and pulled her jacket on. "Find the heron next time before I do."

He watched her go, then unfolded the paper once more and ran his eyes down the column, hunting.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The gym had already been booked for a birthday party the next morning, which meant the end-of-season gathering had to be out of the gym by nine. Sydney stood under the far basket with a roll of masking tape, delimiting the drinks table from the folding chairs, and tried not to look at the scoreboard clock, which someone had left running.

They had lost the semifinal by four points two nights before. Sydney had missed the free throw that would have cut it to two with eleven seconds left, and she had not stopped hearing the sound of the rim, a flat metallic note, like a drawer closing. Now the coach was grilling hot dogs on a rusted cart borrowed from the booster club, and Paityn was stacking paper plates, and everyone was pretending this was only a party and not also a funeral.

The seniors had fifteen hours left, technically, before Parsa left for a campus visit and then, in June, for a university three provinces away. Sydney had done the arithmetic on the bus ride home from the semifinal, staring at the window while Paityn slept against her shoulder. Fifteen hours minus sleep. Less, really. It felt like a number someone had chosen specifically to hurt her.

"Did you know there's a whole theory about this?" she said, when the two of them were alone under the net, shagging balls that no one else would shoot again. "For my psych class I found this thing. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage to the group development model. They called it adjourning. It's for when a group's work ends and members separate."

Parsa caught a ball and held it instead of passing it back. "You're telling me somebody got paid to study why this feels bad?"

"I'm telling you somebody thought it was worth naming." Sydney took the ball from her, more roughly than she meant to, and shot it. It went in clean, which figured. "The other stages are forming, storming, norming, performing. Then in 1977 they added adjourning. Like they'd watched a team before and after and realized the ending was its own thing, not just the absence of the rest."

Parsa was quiet for a moment, and her sullen expression, the one she wore whenever the season was mentioned, softened into something harder to read. "So we're in the fifth stage right now."

"We've been in it since the final buzzer, probably." Sydney retrieved the ball and did not shoot it. "I kept thinking if we'd won, tonight would feel different. But it wouldn't. We'd still be in adjourning. We'd just be in it with a banner."

The coach called them for hot dogs, and there was a ceremony of sorts, paper plates and a cooler and Ms. Byrne, their chemistry teacher, arriving late with a tray of squares she'd baked because she'd heard about the free throw and wanted, in her awkward way, to fix it. Ms. Byrne had never played anything. She sat on the bleachers with the injured reserve guard and asked sincere, unanswerable questions about the pick and roll, and something about her presence made Sydney feel both sorry and grateful, the way you feel about people who care without understanding.

Paityn gave a speech that started as comedy and ended with her voice cracking on the word "seniors," and then everyone pretended to be very interested in the hot dog situation. Later, while the others played a loose half-court game of knockout, Sydney found Parsa by the water fountain, and they talked about whether the theory made it better or worse, having a word for it. Parsa argued it was like relativism, a way of saying nothing really matters because everything is just a stage. Sydney argued the opposite, that naming a thing delimited it, gave it edges, made it something you could walk around and see from all sides instead of drowning in. Neither of them convinced the other, and they left it there, which was its own kind of answer.

At nine the gym monitor came in tapping her watch, and the lights went to half. The seniors took a last lap around the court, barefoot, holding hands, while the juniors stood at center circle and clapped in the ugly fluorescent dimness. Sydney clapped too, thinking that next year she would be the one running the lap, and that some other point guard would be telling some other junior about 1977, and that this was both a comfort and not one at all.

Outside, in the parking lot, Parsa hugged her for longer than their usual. "Text me the thing," Parsa said. "The stages. I want to read the whole model."

"Forming, storming, norming, performing," Sydney said. "Adjourning."

"Adjourning," Parsa repeated, like she was trying the word on, and then she got in her car and sat there a moment without starting it, and Sydney stood in the emptying lot under one flickering sodium light, still holding the game ball she'd walked out with and hadn't noticed picking up.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Under the US Constitution, if the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature.
story:
Natalie set her phone face-up beside her plate, which her mother tolerated on weeknights only if nothing at the table was on fire. The screen showed Congress.gov and a bill she had been following since February, when her civics class had made each of them adopt one and report on its progress like a doctor monitoring a slow heartbeat. Hers was a small thing, a reform of how the government purchased software, and for months it had seemed doomed to die in a subcommittee the way most bills did, unmourned and unremembered.

"So what's the count tonight," her mother said, spooning rice into her brother's bowl without looking up.

"Three hundred and thirty-eight pages of draft text, one amendment in committee, two floor debates, and a vote in both chambers." Natalie scrolled. "It passed the Senate last Thursday. The House took it up today." She said it flatly, because she did not quite believe it. Ms. Sutherland had assigned the bill at random, from a list, and Natalie had resented it at first. Lea-Maude had gotten something about fisheries, which at least sounded alive. Calvin had gotten a defense appropriation, which was practically a coronation. Natalie had gotten procurement reform, the legislative equivalent of watching paint dry in a windowless room.

Her mother asked whether that meant it was a law now. "No," Natalie said. "It goes to the president. He signs it, or he vetoes it." She had habituated herself to the rhythm of the process over the months, the way you learn the schedule of a distant train: introduction, referral to committee, markup, report, debate, vote, other chamber, back again, and finally, if both chambers agreed on the same words, the signature. The signature was the assent, the last door. Calvin had explained that part at lunch with the certainty of someone whose bill had already cleared the House, and she had believed him because he said it like a person who had looked things up.

The chamber vote came through while she was washing dishes. Two hundred and twenty-one to two hundred and four. She stood there with wet hands, reading the tally twice, and felt something embarrassingly close to what Lea-Maude had described when her fisheries bill made it out of subcommittee: proof that a thing could move all the way through the machine without being crushed. Natalie texted Lea-Maude, who replied with nine exclamation points and the question Natalie was already asking herself. Now what? Now the president. Ten days, she remembered dimly, or maybe she was inventing that. She did not text Calvin, because Calvin would explain at length and she wanted to find it herself.

She found it at the dinner table, two evenings later, with the phone propped against the salt shaker because her mother had gone to bed early and her brother was at practice. The tracker said the bill had been presented to the president. Then she refreshed the page and it said something else. Status: became law without a signature. She read the phrase four times. Became law without a signature. Her first thought was that the site was broken. Her second was that she had missed a veto somewhere, some procedural circumlocution buried in a paragraph she'd skimmed. Her third thought was that Calvin had told her the signature was the last door, and Calvin, this once, might be wrong.

She opened the Constitution itself, the actual text, and searched for "bill." There it was, in Article I, plain as a tax form: if the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature. She sat back. The silence of a president could be a kind of consent, as long as Congress was in session and the ten days, not counting Sundays, ran out. It was not a refusal; it was a door left unopened through which the bill walked anyway. She thought about calling Ms. Sutherland, then thought better of it, then thought about how strange it was that a rule this consequential had lived in her textbook's margins while she memorized the flashcards about committee chairs.

The next morning she told Lea-Maude and Calvin at the long table by the cafeteria windows, phone flat between the three of them. "He never signed it," she said. "It became law anyway. Ten days, not counting Sundays, and Congress was in session the whole time." Calvin frowned and pulled out his own phone, and she watched him find the same clause and read it with the expression of a person rearranging furniture in his own head. "Huh," he said finally. "So the signature isn't the last door." Lea-Maude leaned over the screen, chin on her hand. "So he can just say nothing," she said, "and it still happens."

"That's the part I can't decide," Natalie said. "Whether that's a flaw or a feature." She had gone back and forth all night, arguing first that it let a president dodge accountability, then that it kept a single person from strangling a bill through pure inaction, then that maybe both were true at once, which was the most irritating kind of answer and possibly the correct one. She did not know yet. She wrote that down in her project notebook, under the tally and the clause: unresolved. Ms. Sutherland collected the notebooks on Fridays, and Natalie suspected she graded for exactly this, the questions left standing.

That Friday she stayed after class while the room emptied. Ms. Sutherland flipped to her page, read the phrase at the bottom, and looked up. "You going to keep tracking it?" she asked. "The law, I mean. What it actually does now." Natalie had not thought past the signature, or past the absence of one. The implementation hearings were public. The agency had to write the rules. She zipped her bag. "Can I," she said, and Ms. Sutherland slid the calendar of committee dates across the desk.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
Levi had learned the five stages in health class the way other people learn the pledge of allegiance, without questioning who wrote them or why. Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. He kept the list folded in his wallet behind his bus pass, and on the morning of the funeral he checked it twice, the way a boy checks a syllabus before an exam, and found nothing on it that matched how he felt, which was nothing at all. He told himself this was denial. It had to be denial. It was the first one, and he was an orderly person, and he would get through them in order, and by the time school started in the fall he would arrive at acceptance like arriving at a train station, ticket in hand.

His grandmother's house still smelled of her, which is to say of cardamom and old paper, because she had been a judge for thirty years and had never quite retired from jurisprudence, arguing with the letters to the editor right up until the last week. The relatives filled her kitchen now. A garrulous great-uncle occupied the doorway between the kitchen and the hall, telling everyone the story of the flooded cottage in 1996, and everyone let him, because listening to him was easier than talking about her. Levi moved through them with the tray of sandwiches, performing grief's choreography: he accepted a hug, he said thank you, he let Lilianne, who had driven over from her mother's place, hold his elbow for a moment. He was fine. He was completely fine. Anyone watching would have said he was the sturdiest person in the house.

"You're doing that thing," Lilianne said, low, when they'd escaped to the back porch. "The checklist thing. You've got your wallet out."

"It's a model," Levi said. "Five stages. Everybody knows it."

"Kübler-Ross," said a voice behind them, and Makayla came through the screen door with two glasses of lemonade she did not set down. "We did a paper on her last year for psych. Here's the part they don't tell you in health class. The five stages, the whole list, came out in 1969, in her book On Death and Dying, and she wrote it about terminally ill patients facing their own death. Not about the people left behind. Not about you."

Lilianne looked at Levi the way you look at someone who has just been told their map is of the wrong country. Levi, for his part, did not say anything for a long moment, because the porch boards needed studying, and because somewhere underneath his fine-ness a door had come unlatched.

Later that afternoon, Makayla would describe the scene to her own mother on the drive home, and it is her account, not Levi's, that should be trusted here, because Levi had spent the whole week assuring everyone he was fine, and a person that committed to being fine will narrate around the cracks. According to Makayla, he didn't argue. He just stood there with the checklist in his hand, and then he laughed once, short and wrong, and sat down on the steps, and said, "Then what am I supposed to do with this?" And she said she didn't know, and he said, "Nobody ever says they don't know. Everyone's got a pamphlet." And Lilianne sat down on his other side, and the three of them drank the lemonade without toasting anything.

He found the letter while clearing his grandmother's desk, which his aunt had asked him to do because the aunt could not do it. It was in the middle drawer, in the same heavy hand that had underlined half of every law review article she'd ever owned.

Levi. If you are reading this, you are in my house and I am not, which is inconvenient for both of us. Do not let anyone stigmatize whatever your grief turns out to look like, including you. There is no correct order of feelings, any more than there is a correct order of witnesses. You will want a rule. You have always wanted a rule. The closest thing I can give you is this: grieve the way you study, honestly and at your own pace, and ask for help when the material exceeds you. Come back to this house sometimes. The tomatoes need a person.

He put the letter in his shirt pocket, where the checklist had been, and left the wallet on the desk, open, the folded page catching the late light. In the garden the tomato vines had gone wild in ten days, sagging with fruit no one had claimed. He stood at the back door a while, uncertain still, holding both things at once: the list that had told him how to feel, and the fact that it had never been written for him at all. Then he went to the shed, found the shears where she had always kept them, and carried the watering can out between the rows.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: In most jurisdictions traffic already on a highway has the right of way, so a merging driver must adjust speed to fit a gap rather than expect others to make room.
story:
The test was in eleven days, which Edouard announced to the kitchen as though the number itself might do something. His mother kept slicing peppers. Ms. Hussain, who had taught English across the street for thirty years and had agreed to supervise his practice hours because his mother worked nights, looked up from her tea and said, "Eleven days. I once marked thirty essays in eleven days, so I know what despair smells like. It smells like red ink and instant coffee."

They started in the empty lot behind the middle school, where Edouard attempted parallel parking between two traffic cones Deklan had stolen from a road crew, or borrowed, depending on which of them you asked. Deklan sat on the hood of Ms. Hussain's sedan offering commentary in the flat voice of a golf announcer. "He approaches the cone. He reverses. He is now forty centimetres from the curb, which, for those joining us, is a failing distance in every known jurisdiction." Edouard got out and measured it with his shoe. Deklan was right, which was worse than if he had been wrong.

By the fourth evening he could do it, mostly. The trick, if it was a trick, was that the cones stopped being cones. On the first night he had aimed at them as objects, plastic things to avoid; by the fourth he had begun to see the space between them as the thing he was driving into, the gap itself his actual destination. When he said this out loud, Ms. Hussain said it sounded like metonymy, the space standing in for the whole street. Deklan said it sounded like being pretentious about traffic cones. Both positions, Edouard thought, were defensible.

The highway was different. On the sixth evening they took the on-ramp by the industrial park, and Edouard, coming up the merge lane, saw a transport truck in the right lane and simply assumed it would slide left to let him in. He held his speed and waited for the world to rearrange itself around him. The truck did not move. Ms. Hussain said, calmly, the way she used to say "revised draft due Thursday," "Who yields here, Edouard?" He checked the mirror again, braked, tucked in behind the truck, and understood before he finished the manoeuvre that the answer had been him the entire time. Traffic already on the highway had the right of way. He was the one who had to adjust, speed up or slow down to fit whatever gap existed, rather than expect anyone to make room.

He thought about that for the rest of the loop. It struck him as both a rule of the road and something larger, a general principle, though he was wary of principles that instantiated themselves too conveniently in a Tuesday driving lesson. Deklan, when Edouard tried the idea on him at school the next day, waved a fry in disagreement. "So the big truck gets whatever it wants and the little car has to adapt. Cool system. Very fair." Branden, who had failed the test twice and passed on the third attempt, said the rule wasn't about fairness, it was about the fact that you were the one joining something already in motion, and Branden's father drove a truck, so Branden considered the matter settled. Edouard wasn't sure it was settled. Both of them were partly right, and he suspected the rule was less about trucks and small cars than about the simple arithmetic of who was already there.

Two nights before the test, his mother came home early and rode along to the lot. She was effusive in a way she rarely permitted herself, clapping when he parked inside the cones on the first try, and Edouard felt the gain and the cost of it at once: her delight, and the fact that she had been too tired for eleven evenings of it, and that Ms. Hussain had been the one in the passenger seat instead. He parked again, cleanly, and said nothing about any of this.

The morning of the test, the examiner was a woman with a clipboard and the facial expression of a person who had seen every possible way a human being could fail. In the parking phase, Edouard did not think of cones or of metonymy; he thought of the space, and slid into it on the first attempt, close enough to the curb that the examiner made a small check mark. On the road portion she directed him onto the highway. A bus sat in the right lane near the merge. Edouard glanced at the mirror, at the gap behind it, eased off the accelerator, and folded himself into the space the way the space demanded.

Back at the test centre the examiner said he'd passed, and Deklan, who had insisted on waiting in the parking lot with a hand-lettered sign reading CONGRATULATIONS OR CONDOLENCES, held it up without yet knowing which. Edouard rolled down the window and held his temporary licence out through the gap.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
Everyone at the public library knew Zoey was excellent at research papers, mostly because Zoey told them so, usually twice, and Jasmin had once counted.

"You said that already," Jasmin whispered now, sliding into the chair across from her at the corner table by the biography shelves. "In the parking lot. And in the elevator."

"Repetition is emphasis," Zoey said, and squared her two photocopies on the table like duelling biscuits. The assignment, handed down by Mr. Singh, was to compare two scholarly articles on the same question and write a critical review. Not a summary, he had said. A review. He had underlined critical twice on the handout, as if he suspected the whole class of secret summarizing tendencies.

The question her articles answered was whether teens who read on screens sleep worse than teens who read on paper. Article A, from a glossy journal with a confident font, declared that screen readers slept significantly worse and called it a major finding. Article B, dense and dull and full of equations, said the difference between the groups was so small it barely deserved the word difference. Both had used thousands of teenagers. Both had charts. Zoey's first draft, three paragraphs of loyal summarizing, had come back with Mr. Singh's comment in green ink: "Whom do you believe, and why?" She had written "Article A, it's more confident" and then, hearing how that sounded even in her own head, scratched it out.

She remembered, then, the summer she was twelve, when she had told her grandmother that the fortune teller at the county fair knew things because she had guessed Grandma's lucky number. "She guessed a hundred numbers that day," her grandmother had said, patting her hand. "You only remember yours." Zoey had thought it was terribly unfair at the time. The woman wasn't a charlatan; she'd been right, hadn't she? It took Zoey several years and one broken piggy bank to concede otherwise.

Back at the table, Jasmin was reading over her shoulder, which was a violation of the friendship code but a useful one. "Wait," Jasmin said, tapping Article A. "It says significant. Significant means important."

"I thought so too." Zoey turned to the results page and found the numbers, the actual averages for each group's sleep, and subtracted. She subtracted again, because the answer annoyed her. "Look. With thousands of kids in each group, even a difference too small to matter in real life can pass the significance test."

"So it's significant," Jasmin said slowly, "but it's tiny."

"Significant and important aren't the same thing," Zoey said, and felt the floor of the whole glossy confident journal tilt slightly. She had spent three paragraphs calling this finding significant, and it was, technically, and it was also, practically, about as impressive as the fortune teller. She wasn't sure whether she wanted to laugh or write a stern letter to the confident font.

Mr. Singh appeared behind them with a stack of returns balanced on one arm, peered at their table, and raised an eyebrow at the subtraction scrawled across Zoey's notebook margin. "Progress?"

"Article A is trying to prevaricate with statistics," Zoey announced, mostly because she had been saving the word all week. "Or it's just showing off."

"Or it's a specious finding," Jasmin offered. "I've also been saving one."

Mr. Singh set two of the returns down, which was his version of settling in. "So which article wins?"

Zoey looked at the dull one with the equations, which she had dismissed in her first draft as boring and, in the second draft, would have to admit was careful. But B wasn't perfect either; it dragged in extra variables and buried its best point, and she still didn't know whether the screen effect was truly nothing or just truly small, and whether those were even the same thing. She suspected they weren't. She suspected she'd have to write that sentence down and look at it for a while.

"Neither wins," she said. "B's more honest, but A's more readable, which is its own kind of trick. I don't know yet what to do about that."

"Start with what you found out," Mr. Singh said, gathering his stack again. "Uncertainty is a genre. Some of us write in it professionally."

Jasmin waited until he was out of earshot. "So you're not excellent at research papers, then. You're excellent at finding out you were wrong about them."

"That's a promotion," Zoey said, and pulled the draft toward her, crossed out her green-inked green answer, and wrote at the top of a clean page, in handwriting that only wobbled a little: "Both articles are telling the truth. Only one of them is telling the whole truth."
