"Read that out loud when you're done," Jasmin said, stealing a biscuit.

"I'll read it twice," Zoey said. "Repetition is emphasis."

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: NOT EXISTS is another way to find customers with no orders: it keeps each customer for whom a subquery finds no matching order row.
story:
Marcus had the laptop balanced on the arm of the couch, the family room's only lamp throwing his shadow across the coffee table where Kylan sat with his own machine open and Milan sprawled on the rug doing, as far as anyone could tell, nothing at all.

"It's the same answer," Kylan said, turning his screen toward Marcus. "I ran yours and mine. Same eleven customers."

"Then why do they look so different?"

"That's what I'm saying. Who cares?"

Marcus cared, though he couldn't have said why at first. The assignment from Mr. Cheung was simple enough: find every customer in the database who had never placed an order. Marcus had written a query with a LEFT JOIN, checking for rows where the order table came back empty. Kylan had written something else entirely, something with the words NOT EXISTS in it, and the two queries returned the same eleven names in the same order, which felt to Marcus like being handed two keys that opened the same door and being told not to wonder about the locks.

Milan rolled onto his back. "Can we order food? I'm being debilitated by hunger. Genuinely. I can't feel my future."

"You can't feel your future anyway," Kylan said.

"That's the ennui. It's clinical."

Marcus was only half listening. In the flashback that took him, it was two weeks earlier, the first day of the unit, when Mr. Cheung had put the empty database on the projector and said that most of the work of a query happened before you typed a single word. Marcus had thought that was the kind of thing teachers said to sound wise. But he remembered sitting in that classroom, staring at the two tables, customers and orders, and understanding for the first time that the data was a story about people, that somewhere in those rows a customer existed who had signed up and never bought anything, and that his job was to find her, to make the machine say her name.

He scrolled his query to the top of the screen. "Okay, yours. Walk me through what it's doing."

Kylan leaned over, reticent about it in the way he got when he wasn't sure he could defend his own work. "It keeps the customer if nothing comes back."

"Nothing comes back from where?"

"The orders. The part inside." He tapped the screen without touching it, hovering. "For each customer it goes and looks, and if no order row matches, the customer stays. That's it. That's all I did."

"And mine," Marcus said, "keeps everybody and then throws away the ones where the order side came up empty. So we're both throwing people out, just at different times."

"Sure," Kylan said. "Same trash, different bins."

Milan sat up from the rug, which was itself an event. He wanted something, and it wasn't food, though he'd take food. He wanted to be the one who solved something for once. All semester he'd sat in the back of Mr. Cheung's class doing the minimum, and he'd noticed, with a private bitterness he told no one about, that Marcus and Kylan got to be the ones whose screens got projected, whose questions got answered at length. "Run them on the big table," he said. "The one with ten thousand customers. If they're really the same, they should still be the same."

Marcus looked at him. Milan looked back, daring him to say no.

"There's a big table?" Kylan said.

"Mr. Cheung posted it last night. You two were too busy being right to check."

Marcus loaded it, typed his LEFT JOIN version first, and hit enter. The spinner went for a long moment, long enough that Milan said, "It's dying," and then the result appeared: four hundred and twelve customers. He highlighted the query, replaced it with Kylan's, the one with NOT EXISTS, and ran it again. This time the answer came back before he had fully lifted his finger off the key. Four hundred and twelve. The same list, the same silence at the heart of the data, four hundred and twelve people who had walked through the door and bought nothing.

"Faster," Milan said, and there was something in his voice that wasn't envy anymore, or not only envy. "Way faster. Why?"

"I don't know," Marcus said. And it was strange, because he found he liked not knowing. It was like the moment in the flashback again, before the first query, when the data was still just a story he hadn't read yet. He understood what each query did, he could say it out loud, the one kept each customer for whom no matching order row was found anywhere, the other kept everyone and cut the empties afterward, and both of those were true, and both of them gave the same eleven, the same four hundred and twelve, and somewhere past that sameness was a difference he couldn't yet name. Maybe it was speed. Maybe it was something about what happened when the tables got bigger, or when the question changed. He wrote a note to himself in the margin of his notebook: same answer, different question?

Kylan was already closing his laptop, satisfied, because Kylan's want was finished and Kylan had never once in his life been kept awake by a query. "Mr. Cheung's going to ask tomorrow which one we used," he said. "What do we say?"

"We say both," Marcus said. "We say we ran both."

"Then we say which is better."

"We don't know which is better."

"We know which is faster."

"Fast isn't better," Marcus said. "Fast is fast."

Milan pulled his laptop toward himself across the coffee table, opened it, and began, slowly, one finger at a time, to type something of his own. "I'm going to break them," he said. "I'm going to build a table where they don't match."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber mats and lemon disinfectant, and Loic stood at the front desk with a pen in his hand, not writing anything yet. He had saved for four months, bagging groceries after school, because the wrestling coach at the high school had told him he'd need real weight training to make varsity, and the school weight room was closed for asbestos removal until November. The membership form lay between him and the woman behind the desk, Ms. Asante, who had a lanyard with her name printed in small blue letters and a jar of protein bars for sale beside her elbow.

"It's just the standard paperwork," she said, tapping the top page. "Sign at the bottom, initial the boxes."

Loic turned the pages. He was not a fast reader, which embarrassed him in English but which he had decided, somewhere in the last year, was not the same as being a bad reader. He read slowly because he liked to see how sentences were built. The first pages were ordinary: monthly dues, cancellation policy, a forty-dollar fee for lost key cards. Then he reached a dense paragraph headed BINDING ARBITRATION, and he stopped.

"Take your time," Ms. Asante said, though she glanced at the clock, where a spin class would be checking in at five.

The paragraph said that any dispute would be settled through private arbitration instead of in court, and that by signing he waived his right to participate in a class-action lawsuit. He read it twice. He had heard the word arbitration somewhere before, probably in a movie about a baseball player, but he had never seen it in a document with a place for his initials. His mother had signed something like this once, he realized, when she enrolled him in a summer camp after his father left, though she had probably not read it, because she worked nights and read things the way other people swallowed pills, quickly and without looking.

Behind him, the door chimed and Sydnee came in from the cold, still in her scrubs from the veterinary clinic where she interned on Wednesdays. "You're still not signed up? You've been standing here since I walked past the window."

"There's a thing in here," Loic said. "It says if the equipment breaks and I get hurt, I can't sue them in court. It goes to a private arbitrator. And I can't be part of a class action, which I think means a group lawsuit, like everybody who got hurt together."

Sydnee leaned over the desk and skimmed the paragraph. She was better at reading fast than he was, and she had a way of interpolating her own commentary into other people's sentences, so that while he was still forming a thought she had already finished hers. "My sister deals with this at work. Their employment contract has the same clause. She says it's everywhere now, gym contracts, apps, phone plans. Nobody reads them."

"I'm reading it," Loic said.

"That's the problem, you're the only one." She stole a protein bar from the sample jar and Ms. Asante gave her a look that had no real force behind it.

Loic set the pen down. He thought about his biology homework, still in his backpack, a worksheet about how a vaccine trains the immune system by introducing a weakened antigen so the body learns to recognize it later. The contract felt like the opposite of that: something introduced into his life that made him less able to defend himself, not more. It was a strange comparison and he almost said it out loud, but Sydnee was already talking about her shift and the dog that had bitten through a muzzle that afternoon, and the moment passed the way moments did, evanescent, gone before he could hold it.

"Can I take it home?" he asked Ms. Asante. "The contract. To read the rest."

She raised her eyebrows. "In fourteen years, one person has asked me that. A lawyer, and he wanted to know if we validated parking." But she photocopied the pages, and while the machine warmed up she told him her nephew had torn a rotator cuff on a poorly maintained cable machine at another gym, two years ago, and that his case had never reached a judge. "He signed the same kind of paper," she said, handing Loic the copies. "He got some settlement eventually. He wouldn't tell me how much, which told me it wasn't much."

Loic walked home with the pages folded in his jacket. At the kitchen table he read every clause, including the ones about early termination and the waiver of liability for personal injury, which he learned was different from the arbitration clause, though the two sat together on the page like brothers. He understood, by the end, that he had a choice, sort of: he could sign, and train, and accept that if the gym ever wronged him badly he would have to face a private process that the gym had designed for itself; or he could not sign, and keep doing push-ups on the bedroom floor until November, when the asbestos would be gone and the weight room would open for free.

He called Sydnee and told her he was going to sign it anyway, but that he had circled the arbitration clause in pen first, on his copy, so he would remember what he had agreed to. He even understood why he was doing it: the clause was unfair in a small way and useful to him in a large one, and most of being an adult, as far as he could tell, was signing things you hadn't fully chosen. What he could not decide, and told her so, was whether that made him pragmatic or just easy to take advantage of. She said it probably made him both, and that most people were.

The next afternoon he brought the pages back to the front desk. Ms. Asante watched him initial each box in his careful, slow handwriting, and when he reached the signature line she slid the pen holder toward him so it wouldn't roll away. "Varsity, right?" she said.

"Varsity," Loic said, and signed his name, the letters coming out smaller than he expected, all of them fitting easily inside the little gray box.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The night before Eid, Jack sat at the kitchen table while his father counted bills into seven neat stacks, one for each member of the family, including the grandmother who had died in March. "She counts," his father said, not looking up. "The charity is owed for every person in the household, even her, for the days she was alive this year." Jack had always known the money existed, the same way he knew the prayer existed, as furniture in the background of the holiday. Now his father slid the stacks toward him and told him to bag them, because in the morning they would be delivered before the Eid prayer, so that poorer families could celebrate too, and a man who delivered late had defeated the whole point.

"It's called zakat al-fitr," his father said, when Jack asked what to write on the envelope, since the imam liked the envelopes labeled. "A set amount per person. That's the rule."

In the morning Jack drove his father to four houses before the prayer, idling at the curb while his father handed the envelopes through doorways, always with both hands, always refusing tea. At the third house a boy about Jack's age took the envelope and looked at the car, the new rims Jack had bought with his graduation money, and Jack felt something he did not have a word for, a heat that was not exactly shame. His father got back in and said nothing about it, which was somehow worse.

The street festival opened at noon, after the prayer and the long breakfast at his aunt's house, and the whole boulevard smelled of grilled corn and fried dough. Jack had twenty-three dollars of his own in his wallet and a plan for it: the record stall at the far end had a pressing he'd wanted since spring. Daphne texted him twice from the shaved ice stand, and Kaylee was already in line for the ferris wheel, waving with her whole arm the way she did.

He found them under the banners strung between the lampposts, green and gold, turning in the small wind. Daphne was telling Kaylee about their biology final, how the last question had asked them to design a study, and she had proposed comparing genotype data across a screened population, and the teacher had written "ambitious" in red pen and taken off two points anyway. "Ambitious," Kaylee repeated, mock-exasperated. "That's what they say when they mean show off." Jack laughed, but the word sat oddly with him, because that was roughly what his father had said about the rims last month, and Jack had excoriated him for it, told him a man who wanted his son to stay humble forever was a man afraid of his own small life. He had meant it, too, or most of it.

They ate at the epicurean end of the festival, where a stall sold pistachio baklava by the piece and Kaylee insisted on paying for all three. "Eid," she said, as if that explained her, and Jack let her, and watched a family at the next table, the children in new sneakers, matching, the kind of matching that meant someone had bought them all at once, probably this week, probably with the envelopes.

He wanted to believe this was a good thing he was watching. He also wanted his record. He walked toward the stall with the twenty-three dollars and passed a man he recognized from the third house that morning, the father, selling nothing, sitting on the curb with a paper cup of tea, watching the ferris wheel rotate against the sky. Jack stopped. He thought about the set amount per person, the same amount whether the family giving it was comfortable or stretched, the way the rule refused to grade anybody's sacrifice. He thought about Daphne's red-pen "ambitious," and his own speech to his father, and how certainty had felt that night like armor and felt now, remembering the boy's face at the car window, like something he'd worn past its occasion.

He didn't have a theory to offer either direction. That was the honest part. His father believed the giving purified the fast, and maybe it did; Jack only knew that the morning had rearranged something in him without asking permission, and that he distrusted rearrangements that arrived without argument. He sat down on the curb next to the man, who glanced over and seemed, after a moment, to recognize him too.

Jack took out the twenty-three dollars, held it a second, then held it out. "For Eid," he said. "For your kids' sneakers, whatever you want." The man looked at the money and then at Jack's face for a long moment, and Jack understood that this could go two ways, that pride was not a smaller thing in other households than in his own, and that he had not thought this far ahead.

The man took the bills, folded them once, and put them in his shirt pocket, and said, "Get back to your friends, they're looking for you." Jack turned. Kaylee and Daphne were standing at the edge of the crowd, one holding shaved ice, the other pointing at the record stall, and the line for the ferris wheel had just started moving.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller, and shrank further after accounting for family background.
story:
Cohen had been shelving the cough syrup for eleven minutes when his grandfather appeared at the counter of Zhou's Pharmacy, holding a bag of peppermints like evidence. The bell above the door was still trembling. Outside, the November light was going thin and yellow over the parked cars, and Mr. Zhou was in the back unpacking boxes of gauze, so it was Cohen who rang up the mints, and Cohen who had to listen.

"Your mother says you're thinking of spending your savings," his grandfather said. "On a car."

"A cheap one. I'd keep the job through spring, maybe longer." Cohen slid the mints into a paper bag with the care he gave prescriptions, folding the top twice, because Mr. Zhou had shown him how and had never needed to show him twice.

"You know about the marshmallow study," his grandfather said. It wasn't a question. He leaned on the counter the way he leaned on the fence at home, forearms down, weight forward. "Kids who could wait for a second marshmallow did better later. Everything, school, jobs. It's character, Cohen. Waiting is character." He tore the bag open before Cohen could, and a mint clicked against his teeth.

Cohen had read about that study the year before, in Mr. Zhou's waiting room, in a magazine so old its cover had faded. He had read past the famous part. "There was a replication in 2018," he said. "Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan, Haonan Quan. They found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller than the original, and it shrank further once they accounted for family background."

His grandfather stopped chewing. Behind them, boxes thumped in the stockroom.

"So you're saying waiting means nothing."

"No." Cohen wiped the counter, though it wasn't dirty, because there was a smudge near the register that had been there since September and he'd decided today it would go. "I'm saying the kids who could wait were usually the kids who already had reasons to trust that the second marshmallow was coming. Their waiting made sense." He worked the smudge in a slow circle. "You taught me to save. That's not nothing. But you had steady work your whole life. Somebody like Raphael..." He stopped, because the bell rang, and Raphael himself came in with his backpack over one shoulder and frost in his hair.

Raphael worked Tuesdays and Thursdays, the closing shift, and he was saving for nothing as far as anyone could tell; he spent his paychecks on takeout and a phone case that lit up when it rang. He bought a soda now, counting out coins with cold fingers, and stayed to talk by the magazine rack, and Cohen watched his grandfather watch Raphael the way a man appraises a machine that runs loud. After Raphael left, his grandfather said, "That boy won't wait for anything," and it wasn't cruel, exactly. It was the sound of a conclusion arriving early, the way conclusions did in his family, with a click like a stamped form.

"You don't know that," Cohen said. "You met him for four minutes." He thought of Veronica, who tutored Raphael in chemistry for free every Saturday, who had told Cohen once, without drama, that Raphael's mother took his paycheck for rent and he made it back by eating at other people's houses. Whether that was true Cohen didn't know. Veronica was honest but she was also loyal, and loyalty can burnish a story the way a cloth burnishes silver, until you can't tell the metal from the shine.

His grandfather turned his hat in his hands. "All I'm saying is the future comes for you whether you plan for it or not."

"That's fair," Cohen said, and meant it. The car would cost half his savings. The savings were for college, in a town where the college fund was a coffee can his mother labeled with a joke and then stopped joking about. He could keep taking the bus at six-forty every morning, rain or otherwise, and keep the money whole; or he could buy the Buick from Veronica's uncle and take more shifts, and maybe lose the thread entirely if the transmission went. Both arguments felt true. He had spent two weeks trying to make them into one true thing and had not managed it, and he suspected the honest position was the one he was standing in: sure that waiting mattered, unsure how much, unable to prove it either way.

Mr. Zhou came out of the stockroom with a box cutter in his hand and studied the two of them, the closed paper bag, the space where the smudge had been. "The counter looks good," he said to Cohen. Then, to the grandfather, "He's careful with the register. Careful and fast, which is rare." He went back to his boxes, and Cohen's grandfather looked at the counter as if it had said something, and put his hat on.

"I'll think about the study," his grandfather said. "You think about the car." He pushed through the door with the bell clattering behind him, and through the glass Cohen watched him pause at the curb, hand raised, checking both ways down the empty street before he crossed.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s.
story:
The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered phone repair shop, its window plastered with posters of beaches Levi had no interest in. He had come for a ticket to Tokyo, one way, leaving in forty hours, because the exchange program had emailed at nine that morning to say his placement was confirmed and his documents had to be booked by Friday or forfeited. Mr. Goh, who owned the agency and had apparently owned it since before Levi was born, was clicking through fares on a monitor older than the shop's paint while Levi waited, his notebook open on the counter.

The notebook was the problem, or rather what was in it. On the flight-out paperwork the program wanted a short essay, due by Monday, on how Japan's demographics might shape daily life for an exchange student. Mr. Goh's printer had produced the sheet, and stapled to it was a population pyramid of Japan that Levi had stared at for ten minutes without understanding. The shape was all wrong for what he pictured a pyramid to be. It bulged near the top, thick in the fifties and sixties, and narrowed toward the bottom where the children were, so that it looked less like a monument than like a barrel balanced on a stem.

"Half fare or full?" Mr. Goh asked, scrolling. "You turn nineteen on the plane?"

"Eighteen," Levi said. "Born in March."

"March." Mr. Goh wrote something on a pad. "So you're the bottom of their pyramid, more or less. The narrow part."

Levi looked up. "You know about these?"

"I sell tickets to Japan four times a month. You learn what the country looks like." Mr. Goh turned his monitor so Levi could see a government chart on it. "About 29 percent of the people there are 65 or over, early 2020s numbers. Near a third of the whole country. One of the oldest populations in the world."

Levi wrote the number down, then sat with it, because a number by itself told him nothing. A third of the country was old. He tried to imagine his own street, his own school, remade in those proportions, and found he couldn't, so he tried it a different way, the way his geography teacher had nagged them to: if the bars run thick at the top, what does the country need more of, and what does it need less of? Nursing homes, he thought. Hospitals. Ramps. Fewer kindergartens. But then a doubt arrived, quiet and unwelcome: a fat bar of sixty-year-olds today becomes a fat bar of eighty-year-olds in twenty years, and a thin bar of children today becomes a thin bar of parents, and then who staffs the nursing homes? The pyramid predicted, but it predicted in layers, each one a guess stacked on a guess.

The door chime rang and Matthieu came in with Loic behind him, still in their soccer gear, smelling of the field. They had come from practice and had somehow heard, through the team's group chat, that Levi was flying out Saturday.

"Saturday," Matthieu said, as if the word itself were an accusation. "You told us September."

"It moved. There was a cancellation." Levi covered his notebook, then uncovered it, because hiding it was a kind of lie and he was tired of those. "I have to write about this pyramid thing before Monday. Tell me what you see." He slid the chart across the counter.

Loic leaned on the glass with both elbows, truculent even at rest, the way he was after losses, and their match had apparently been one. "I see a country running out of kids," he said. "So it's dying. Write that."

"It's not dying," Levi said. "That's the first thing I got wrong. It's aging. Those aren't the same."

Matthieu tapped the wide band at the pyramid's middle. "These people, though, the fifty-year-olds. They're the ones doing everything right now. Running the trains, teaching, whatever. In twenty years they need the care, and there's fewer people behind them." He looked at Levi with a small shrug, offering it rather than insisting.

Levi took the chart back and turned it over, and on the blank side he drew two crude pyramids side by side. Under the first, Japan's, he wrote "schools? nursing homes?" with an arrow slanting from schools toward nursing homes. Under the second he drew his own country's shape, wider at the base, and reversed the arrow. Two countries, two needs, and he was beginning to see that the question wasn't which one to answer but how a person reads the shape honestly, without letting the answer flatter whatever he already believed. He had caught himself, earlier that week, wanting to write something dramatic about a fading nation, mostly because drama aggrandized the writer, and he suspected the essay would survive better without that.

"You're doing homework in a travel agency," Loic said, but he said it without heat, and when Mr. Goh slid a printed fare across the counter, Loic read the price and stopped complaining about anything.

Levi looked at the ticket. Saturday, one way, a departure time in the afternoon that would put him over the Pacific while his classmates were at practice. The money was his father's, or mostly his father's, with some of his own from the summer job folded in, and signing for it felt less like buying travel than like agreeing to be changed by it.

"One thing," Mr. Goh said, taking back his pen. "When you get there, you'll be in a place full of old people by your standards. Don't write about it like it's a tragedy. It's just a fact with a shape. Read the shape." He was already turning to his screen, the transaction done, the advice delivered as if it were a baggage allowance.

Levi copied his two pyramids into the notebook properly, and beneath them he wrote a line he thought he might keep: the pyramid tells you what a country will need, but not when, and not who pays. That much he was sure of. The rest, how a third of a country aged 65 and over actually lived, what it felt like on a Tuesday morning in a neighborhood he couldn't yet name, he left as a question, honestly open, because he would be there by Sunday and could find out.

Matthieu read over his shoulder and pointed at the question. "That's the good part," he said. "The part you don't know yet."

Levi closed the notebook, put the ticket in his inside pocket, and pressed it flat with his hand. "Saturday," he said. "Two in the afternoon. Both of you can come to the airport or not, but I'm buying the coffee either way."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
story:
The envelope sat between the salt shaker and a stack of her mother's flashcards, and Makayla knew what it was before she opened it. She had used the card exactly twice: forty dollars in gas for the drive to the college visit, and then, on the last night of that trip, the boots. Two hundred and eighty dollars, tan leather, reduced from three hundred forty. She had told herself she would pay it off with her next two paychecks from the garden center, but the envelope had arrived before the second paycheck, and the number inside was now real in a way it hadn't been at the register.

"Minimum payment: twenty-five dollars," she read aloud, because saying it made it smaller. The full balance, printed a few lines above, was three hundred twenty-one and change. She turned the statement over, where the fine print ran in gray columns, and her mother looked up from a card that read antigen on one side and provoked an immune response on the other.

"You're mumbling," her mother said.

"Twenty-five dollars. That's all they want."

Her mother set the card down and pulled her coffee closer, the way she did every night before her exam studies, some small epicurean ritual with the good mug and the steam held under her nose. "Want is an interesting word for it," she said, and went back to the flashcards.

Makayla pulled up her banking app under the table. Savings: one hundred ninety-four dollars and twelve cents. Below that, in smaller green text, a line she usually ignored: interest earned this quarter, $1.61. She stared at it. Her money, sitting there, had made a dollar sixty-one without her touching it. Meanwhile the card wanted her money to shrink if she only gave it a little at a time, though she couldn't have said exactly how that worked, and the fine print on the back of the statement was written in a language designed, she suspected, to be reread.

She texted Everett, who had gotten his own card in the spring and had opinions about everything. Bill came, she typed. 321. I have 194. Pay the minimum or empty my savings?

His reply came fast: minimum. that's what it's for. His second text came faster: wait. does yours have a grace period?

She typed what is that and then deleted it, because she could find out herself. The word was on the statement's back, third paragraph, buried between late fees and balance transfers. She ran her finger under the sentences while her mother shuffled flashcards and muttered about antigens and antibodies, and what she found was this: if she paid the full balance by the due date each month, they charged her nothing on the new purchases. Nothing. The twenty-five dollar minimum was a door that looked like an exit, and if she walked through it, the free part was gone.

She called Everett instead of texting. "So if I pay all of it, on time, they don't add anything?"

"That's the whole game," he said. "I learned it the bad way. I paid the minimum for two months on a skateboard and ended up paying for the skateboard plus a fee on the skateboard. My sister called it a tax on not reading."

"Then why does the minimum exist?"

"It exists for the month you genuinely can't. It's not a plan, it's a parachute." She heard his television in the background, someone shouting about a fumble. "You have the money, right? Pay it and be done."

She did have the money, most of it. That was the part that pinched. The savings had taken a year, ten dollars from each paycheck sometimes, twenty when the hours were good, and it had grown the way things grow slowly: by deposits, and then, recently, by that small green interest that she now understood was the same force pointed in the opposite direction. Money you owed could swell against you. Money you kept could swell for you. It felt like learning that water ran downhill and uphill, depending on which side of the hill you stood on.

Her mother was on the last stack of cards, the good mug nearly empty. Makayla did not have the temperament to sit and introspect about it; she wanted the thing decided. She set the phone down, opened the card's payment page, and typed the full number: 321.16. The confirmation asked if she was sure, as if it were doing her a kindness by checking.

"I'm paying the whole thing," she said out loud. "If I pay it all by the due date, they can't charge me for the purchases."

Her mother looked up, one eyebrow moving a fraction. "Good. Now you know something most people learn at thirty." She tapped a flashcard against the table. "Hand me that mug, and tell me why I shouldn't buy you another pair of boots as a reward."

Makayla carried the mug to the sink and ran the water until it went hot over her hands. On the counter, her phone lit with the payment confirmation, and behind it her banking app still showed the savings account, thinner now by three hundred twenty-one dollars, already earning its first fraction of a cent on what was left. She dried her hands on the dish towel and went back to the table, where her mother had dealt the flashcards between them like a hand of cards, antigen side up, waiting.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
Naomi had the voter registration page open on the family laptop for forty minutes before she touched the keyboard. The kitchen was quiet except for the refrigerator's hum, and the light through the window had gone the colour of weak tea. Her mother had left a note about dinner, and beside the note, unopened, an envelope from Elections Canada with her name on it, spelled correctly, which somehow made the whole thing more real than the website did.

She texted Adem first, because Adem had opinions about everything and because she wanted one of them before she started forming her own. He answered with a voice memo, as usual, three minutes long, mostly about the riding boundaries being redrawn so that his street had moved into a different district than his cousin's, though they lived six houses apart. "It's gerrymandering," he said, and then, quieter, "Or it's not, actually, I looked it up, we don't really do that here the same way. But it feels like something." Naomi smiled at that. Adem's convictions always ran ahead of his research, but he circled back, which she respected.

She typed her name into the form and then stopped at the date of birth field. Eighteen. It was strange to see the number she'd been waiting for all year reduced to a box you filled in. She typed it and the page accepted it without ceremony, without a bell or a banner, and she felt vaguely cheated. Somewhere in her mind she had imagined a threshold, a door you pushed through, and instead there was only the next field, her address, which she knew by heart.

The question arrived in her head the way small questions do, sideways. She wondered how long eighteen-year-olds had been allowed to do this at all. She opened a new tab and typed it out plainly, not even sure what she expected. Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970. She read the sentence twice. Nineteen seventy. Before her mother was born, but not by much; after her grandmother had already had three children. It meant that when her grandmother was Naomi's age, standing in some kitchen with her own first baby, she could not have voted. Naomi sat with that. Fifty-odd years, which sounded long as a number and short as a life.

She texted Harlow, who was the sort of person who kept a spreadsheet of every party's platform points and rated them for honesty. "Did you know it was only 1970," Naomi typed, "when they lowered the voting age from 21 to 18?" Harlow replied within a minute: "Yes. Also my grandmother still doesn't vote because she says one election never changed anything for her, which is the most depressing thing anyone in my family says." Then: "Are you registering finally or just reading history." Naomi typed "both" and went back to the form.

The secondary question, the one the form actually asked, was whether she wanted to be affiliated with a party for the purposes of nomination contests. She had gone into the evening thinking she knew the answer. Harlow's spreadsheet had effectively decided it for her, Harlow being persuasive in the way of people who have done the work and expect you to benefit from it. But Adem's voice memo was still in her ears, his irritation at being moved between ridings like a chess piece, his sense that the system arranged people rather than representing them. She did not think Harlow was wrong. She did not think Adem was wrong either. She thought they were both describing something true from different windows.

She went out to the porch to clear her head, and Ms. Nkosi was watering her pots next door, the late ones, the chrysanthemums she'd put in against her son's advice. "You look like someone doing taxes," Ms. Nkosi said. "Worse," Naomi said. "Voting." Ms. Nkosi laughed and said she'd vote in every election until they buried her, because in the country where she grew up she had queued for six hours once and been turned away, and she had promised herself then that she would never again treat a ballot as a chore. Naomi asked whether she'd ever voted for a winner. "Once or twice," Ms. Nkosi said. "It was less satisfying than I expected." She pinched a dead bloom off the chrysanthemum and dropped it into her apron pocket.

Back inside, Naomi finished the form. She chose the party affiliation, but she did it her own way: not because Harlow's spreadsheet ranked it highest, and not as a gesture against Adem's cynicism, but because she had read two planks of its platform herself, the student grant one and the housing one, and found she could live inside both. She put her putative support on record knowing it was provisional, a first position rather than a final one, and she was honest with herself that she might change it in two years, or in four, and that this would not make her fickle. It would make her eighteen, and then twenty-two, and then older.

She paid the five-dollar fee for the nomination membership out of her own account, the account her grandfather had set up, telling her it was a kind of annuity, small deposits now so there would be something steady later. She had always thought of it as his way of acceding to her mother's spending habits without saying so, money as a peace offering. It felt right that this was the money buying her first membership card, his patience funding her first decision.

The confirmation email arrived while she was closing tabs. She forwarded it to Harlow, who responded with a screenshot of the riding map and the words "you're in Adem's old district now, congratulations, your vote is worth exactly as much as his." Naomi was still laughing at that when Adem's next voice memo came through, four minutes this time. She pressed play, and the first thing she heard was her own name, followed by: "So I re-read the boundaries, and I was wrong, we're in the same riding after all, I've been ranting at my cousin for nothing." She put the laptop to sleep and sat in the dark kitchen, listening.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome sat on the windowsill of Mr. Kang's studio, a wooden pyramid with a brass pendulum, and it had not been wound in years. Elliot noticed it on his fourth lesson, because by then he had begun noticing everything in the room: the taped seam on the bench cushion, the pencil marks in the Beethoven, the way Mr. Kang's chair never quite faced the piano. He was eighteen and had started lessons late, after his grandfather died and left him the upright piano from the house on Cormorant Street, along with the feeling that learning to play it was something he owed a man he had never quite known.

The problem was rhythm. Mr. Kang said it once, plainly, without cruelty, and made Elliot play the C major scale against the digital metronome on the phone. Elliot's eighth notes swam. They hurried when the music got easy and dragged when it got hard, and he could hear himself doing it and could not stop.

"You count with your feelings," Mr. Kang said. "The phone counts with nothing."

That evening Elliot went back to Cormorant Street, where his mother was sorting the last of the boxes. The old metronome was in the study, wrapped in a dish towel, and when he lifted the pendulum out of its bracket and set it ticking against his palm, the weight of it surprised him. He brought it to the next lesson in his backpack, and when he set it on the music rack, Mr. Kang stopped talking mid-sentence and looked at it for a long moment.

"It was my grandfather's," Elliot said. "I looked it up. Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, but the design was really Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel's. Maelzel basically took it from him." He had read it two nights before, chasing the name stamped inside the case, and had thought about it since: a man building a machine to keep perfect time, and the argument over whose time it was.

Mr. Kang wound the mechanism, and the old pendulum began to tick, a wooden sound, softer than the phone. "Winkel got a medal eventually," he said. "Not the patent. Play your scale against it." He did not say anything else about the history, and Elliot, watching the brass weight travel, decided this was not evasion. It was a kind of respect.

Elliot played, and the wooden tick changed something, though not what he expected. The phone's beep had made him obedient and brittle; he followed it the way a prisoner follows a fence. The old metronome he argued with. Its tick had a faint grain to it, and when he pushed ahead or fell behind, he could hear the disagreement in the room instead of just in his own hands. Mr. Kang sat with his arms folded and let the argument run for a full two scales before he spoke.

"Better," he said. "Not accurate. Better."

They worked like that through October. Elliot practiced at Cormorant Street with the metronome on the windowsill of the study, and on Thursdays he carried it across town to the studio. Caylee, who had taken lessons since she was seven and played a Chopin waltz the way other people breathed, told him he was being a reactionary about it. "A phone app does the same thing," she said, waiting on the studio's bench for her own lesson. "Wood doesn't keep better time. It keeps worse time and you like the sound." Elliot said maybe, and did not give the metronome up, and did not fully disagree with her either, which she pointed out was the most irritating position a person could hold.

The metronome stopped on a Thursday in November. Not gradually; between one lesson and the next, the spring would not hold its tension, and the pendulum swung twice and settled. Elliot opened the back panel on the studio table while Mr. Kang made tea, and found the cord frayed through, not snapped but worn, worn in a way that looked deliberate, a knife drawn along the fibers until they gave. He did not say anything for a moment. He thought of Kinley, who had been at the studio the previous Thursday, filling in for Caylee's canceled slot, and who had spent the whole hour arguing that the metronome was a crutch, that real musicians internalized time and didn't lean on some nineteenth-century gadget.

Mr. Kang came back with two cups and looked at the cut cord, then at Elliot, and Elliot understood that he was being offered something. He could accuse Kinley. He could say nothing. The evidence was real but thin, and Kinley had been vocal, not violent, as far as Elliot knew. Mr. Kang had not touched the metronome, had been across the room; the tea was not an alibi so much as a courtesy, though it did quietly exonerate him, and Elliot noticed himself doing that accounting, weighing who had been where, and disliked the taste of it.

"Grandpa's metronome," he said finally. "A hundred years of ticking and it dies in a studio in November." He turned the pendulum weight in his fingers, the small brass block his grandfather had set to the same marking, according to the penciled note inside the case, every day for decades. "I can get the cord replaced. My mom knows a clock guy." He set the pieces back in the panel and closed it. "I'm not going to ask who did it. If it was an accident, asking insults somebody. If it wasn't, asking makes me a detective instead of a student."

Mr. Kang drank his tea. "Then play," he said, and pulled the phone across the table, set it ticking at sixty, and opened the Beethoven to the page with the penciled marks. Elliot put his hands on the keys, phone flat on the rack where the pyramid used to sit, and began, and for the first time the beep was not a fence but a question, one he answered a little differently every bar.

The following Thursday the metronome was back on the windowsill, wound and ticking, and Kinley was already inside, playing something slow and unsteady with no accompaniment at all. When Elliot came through the door, Kinley looked up from the keys and did not stop playing, and the two times ran side by side in the room, brass and wood, and neither of them said a word about it.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Katherine's father had made his epicurean Sunday dinner again, the one with the butter-braised leeks and the chicken he browned in a pan older than she was, and for a while the table ran on its usual rails: her mother recounting the neighbour's fence dispute, her little brother negotiating for extra potatoes. Then her father raised his glass and said, "To your first election, anyway. Tomorrow you become a citizen in the full sense."

"Tomorrow," Katherine said, and the word landed strangely, the way a familiar room looks wrong when a picture has been moved. She had turned eighteen in March. She had followed the campaign, had argued about the leaders' debate with Esteban at lunch until Ms. Morales told them to take it to the hallway. But when she tried to picture the actual act, card in hand, curtain behind her, she could not remember ever registering. No form, no envelope, no confirmation. Her brother, thrilled to be the bearer of bad news, said that if you weren't registered you couldn't vote, everyone knew that.

"I don't think that's true," her mother said, but in the tone of someone hoping rather than knowing. Her father was already frowning at his chicken. Katherine took her phone into the pantry, where the light was bad but the privacy was good, and called Audrey-Anne, who had voted... no, Audrey-Anne didn't turn eighteen until June. She called anyway, because Audrey-Anne read everything, including the parts of the internet nobody else had patience for.

"I never got anything in the mail," Katherine said. "Not a card, nothing. Did you get a card?"

"I'm seventeen, Katherine, I get a report card." Audrey-Anne's keyboard clattered in the background, and then stopped. "Okay, so don't panic. My aunt worked as a poll worker. If you're not on the voters list, you can still register at your polling place on election day. You just bring ID with your address. Where's your polling place?"

Katherine pressed her forehead against the pantry shelf, beside the cans of tomatoes. "I don't even know that."

"Then that's your homework for tonight. And take a utility bill, or something with your address. Your health card isn't enough on its own, I think. Bring two things. Bring everything."

Back at the table, her brother was still going, explaining to their father how elections worked, and her father was nodding along in the loose way he nodded when he wasn't listening. Katherine sat down, folded her napkin, and interrupted. "You can register at the polling station on election day. If you're not on the list. So it's fine." She said it flatly, like the weather, and watched her brother deflate by degrees. Her mother reached over and squeezed her wrist, once, and said nothing, which in their family meant a great deal.

Later, at the window, Katherine watched the lake behind their houses undulate under the last wind of the evening, grey going to black, and Esteban's porch light across the water. He texted her: polls open 7. walking over at 7:15 if you want company. She thought about how little a single vote was, one mark among thousands in this riding alone, and how her father had once called the ballot a synecdoche, a small standing piece for a larger thing, and how she had rolled her eyes at the time. She was still not sure he was right. One vote might just be one vote. But she set her health card, her student card, and a printed hydro bill on the desk chair by the door, and she set her alarm for six-thirty, which was a thing she could be sure of.

The school gymnasium smelled of floor wax and coffee. At a table just inside the doors, a woman with a lanyard asked for Katherine's address, found her polling station number on a laminated map, and pointed her to the far corner. There, at a foldout table marked with a paper sign, a second poll worker took her documents, copied the address onto a form, and slid it across for a signature. "You weren't on the list," the woman said, "but you are now. Line's short, go ahead."

In the cardboard booth, the pencil on its string, Katherine stood for a moment longer than she needed to. She thought of Esteban waiting outside, of Audrey-Anne's keyboard clattering, of her brother's face when she'd told him it was fine. She made her mark, folded the paper, and fed it into the box. The poll worker tore a strip off her registration form and said, "You'll be on the list next time." Katherine pushed through the doors into the cold bright morning, where Esteban was hopping foot to foot on the frost. "Well?" he said. She held up her purple-stained finger. "Now I get breakfast."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
Antoine had decided he was excellent at eye contact, which was the first sign that he was not. He practiced on the swings at the playground behind the school, where Timothy and Jaskaran had agreed to run mock interviews before Antoine applied at the deli on Marsh Street. He fixed his gaze on Timothy with such intensity that Timothy stopped mid-question and said, "You're staring like I owe you money."

"Blinking is weakness," Antoine said. "The internet said so."

"The internet also said you could train your hairline," Jaskaran said from the slide, where he sat with his phone, pretending to be the manager but mostly scrolling. He looked up long enough to deliver the first real question. "Why do you want this job?"

The honest answer was that his mother's hours at the clinic had been cut and the fall tuition deposit was due in August, but that felt like too much to hand a stranger across a counter. He tried the rehearsed line instead, about customer service and growth, and heard Timothy mutter "pugnacious" under his breath, which Antoine chose to interpret as a compliment though he suspected it was not. He delivered the answer a second time anyway, slower, and this time it sounded less like a hostage statement.

Then Mr. Rowe came through the playground with his dog, as he did every afternoon, and stopped when he heard the word "deli." He had worked at the school long enough that he knew which students had money and which didn't, and he asked no questions about either. "They'll want you on the slicer by week two," he said. "Everyone starts on dishes, then the slicer." The dog transfixed by a squirrel at the fence, Mr. Rowe walked on, and Antoine sat down on the swing because his legs had gone strange.

He had read something, or half-read something, in the pamphlet from the career office that he'd folded into his back pocket and ignored. He took it out now, smoothing it on his knee while Jaskaran read over his shoulder. There it was, in small print: workers aged sixteen and seventeen had no limit on working hours. No limit at all. He could close every night if he wanted. But the next sentence said they might not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor had declared hazardous. He read the line twice. "So the hours are fine," he said slowly, "but the slicer might not be."

"Meat slicers," Jaskaran said, tapping his phone, holding up a page that listed them among the hazardous occupations. "It's a whole list. Slicers, some machines, roofing." Timothy leaned over and said, "Wait, so they can work you unlimited hours but not near a meat slicer?" Antoine nodded, and the three of them sat with that for a moment, the weirdness of it. A seventeen-year-old could be trusted with a forty-hour week, or more, but not with a blade that spun. He wondered whether that was protection or insult, and could not decide, and found he liked the not-deciding, the way a fact could sit there with two possible feelings attached to it.

The unreliable part, the part Antoine kept revising in his own memory even as it happened, was what he did next. He would later tell himself he marched into the deli that evening with total confidence, but what actually happened was that he stood outside for four minutes rehearsing, walked in, and asked the man at the counter whether the person they hired would be running the slicer. The man said probably, eventually. Antoine heard his own voice go thin and then steadier: "I'm seventeen. Sixteen and seventeen year olds can work any hours, but we can't be put on jobs the Department of Labor calls hazardous. Slicers are on the list." The man stopped stacking cheese and looked at him with an expression Antoine could not read, somewhere between annoyed and impressed, and said, "Nobody's ever asked that."

"Is the job still open?" Antoine asked, and held his eyes, blinking at normal intervals, hands still in his pockets where they'd been squeezing his fists the whole time. The man pulled an application from under the register and set it on the counter between them, and behind him the slicer sat clean and unplugged, catching the fluorescent light.

fact: In October 2024 the Los Angeles Times did not endorse a presidential candidate after its owner blocked the editorial board's plans, and several board members resigned in protest.
story:
The espresso machine hissed while Stella spread the proofs across the corner table, weighting the front page with her mug. The headline read WATER TESTS DELAYED AT DISTRICT STADIUM, and beneath it Coraline's byline sat above eight hundred words about a plumbing contract awarded to a company whose paperwork nobody at the district would produce. The paper went to print Thursday. It was Tuesday, and the principal's email had arrived an hour ago asking Stella to stop by before lunch.

"Read it again," Coraline said. She was folding napkins into triangles, not looking at the page.

"'Given the sensitivity of pending contractual matters, I'd ask that we discuss the timing of this article.' That's the whole email. That's not a discussion. That's a warning shot."

Taya came in shaking rain off her jacket and dropped into the third chair without asking what the meeting was about, because she'd been in the group chat all morning. "So delay it. Run it after the season ends."

"Then it's not news, it's a memoir." Stella turned her mug a quarter turn, then another quarter. "The playoff game is Friday. If the water testing got pushed, people are sitting in that stadium in three days."

"Her dad works for the district," Coraline said quietly. "That's the part she isn't saying."

Taya's chin came up. "That's not the part I'm not saying. The part I'm not saying is that we're seventeen and eighteen and nobody at this table has a lawyer."

Stella pulled out her phone and scrolled to the screenshot she'd saved in September, back when she'd been drafting her college essay about why she wanted to be a journalist. She'd gone down a rabbit hole one night and found the whole thing again this morning on the bus. "You know what the LA Times did in October 2024?" she said. "Nothing. They didn't endorse anybody for president. The editorial board had a plan to, and the owner blocked it, and several board members resigned over it."

"Resigned," Coraline repeated. "From the LA Times."

"From the LA Times. Actual grown-ups with actual careers walked out because the person who owned the paper decided what it could say." Stella set the phone face-down. "And our situation is a thousand times smaller, and Dr. Patel isn't an owner, but the shape is the same. Whoever controls the printing decides what's printable. I keep thinking it doesn't count because we're a school paper, and then I keep thinking that's exactly when it counts."

Taya sat back with her arms crossed. "So your plan is to be a martyr at a high school with fifteen hundred students."

"My plan is to not decide in the hallway. I'm going to the meeting first." Stella gathered the proofs into her bag, squaring the edges against the table. For a second the whole front page transfigured in her mind into something braver than it was, a document that would be studied rather than recycled, and she made herself shrink it back to what it actually was: eight hundred words by her friend about pipes.

The meeting was short. Dr. Patel talked about liability, about the district's legal review, about not wanting students to be the ones carrying risk that belonged to adults. Stella asked one question, whether the district was asking her to delay the story or telling her to, and Dr. Patel folded her hands and said the district was confident she'd make a responsible choice. Stella said thank you and left before her face could show anything.

At the coffee shop that evening she found Coraline alone at the same table, one untouched cocoa, the proofs still in the bag. "It's still my call," Stella said. "She never said stop. She said responsible." Coraline waited. Outside the window the rain had stopped and the street had turned glossy, reflecting the shop lights like something impermeable laid over the town, a skin nothing got through. Stella thought of the resignations in Los Angeles, people who'd left rather than print silence, and thought too of Taya's father and the playoffs and the fact that she would be gone by September, living this town's news secondhand. In philosophy class they'd spent two weeks on existentialism, the idea that the choice is yours whether or not you want it, and she'd written in her notebook that it sounded exhausting. It was less abstract now.

She opened the bag, took out the front page, and laid it on the table between them, and slid her mug off the corner.

"Thursday," she said. "As is."

Coraline looked at the page, then at her. "I'll fix the typo in the third graph tonight."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, while an endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter.
story:
Hannah's grandmother had one rule about the dining room table: whoever used it for homework had to wipe it down before dinner, no exceptions, even during a crisis. Hannah was having a crisis. The paper was due Monday morning at eight, it was Sunday at two, and the word processor on her laptop had just done something to her notes that she could not undo.

She had spent the whole weekend at the house because her parents were painting her room, and her grandmother's internet worked only if you sat in the corner of the porch near the kitchen window, holding the tablet at a certain angle like a divining rod. Ilan had sent her three texts about the assignment, each more morose than the last, and Thea had sent one, which read simply: "mine is done." That was Thea. She had written hers in two evenings and then gone to a movie while the rest of the class suffered.

The paper itself was in decent shape, Hannah thought. The prompt was whether school rankings created a true meritocracy or just the appearance of one, and Hannah had argued, with actual evidence she'd found at the library before coming out here, that ranking students measured preparation as much as talent. She had a quotation from a sociologist, a statistic from a school district report, and a counterargument she'd stolen, in spirit, from an argument with Ilan, who believed that competition sorted people fairly and that complaining about it was sour grapes. She'd put his position in the paper more sympathetically than he'd put it himself, which had felt, at the time, like a small act of generosity.

The problem was the notes. She had inserted them one by one, all morning, imagining them sitting at the bottom of each page where she'd used the source. Then she'd scrolled to check her formatting, and every single note had migrated. They were all stacked together on the last page like passengers herded into one car of a train.

She called Ilan. He answered on the second ring, sounding like someone who had been staring at a screen for hours. "Is yours broken too?" she asked. "My notes all moved to the end. All of them. I put them on the pages and they went to the end."

"That happened to mine," Ilan said. "I think it's a glitch."

"It's not a glitch," said her grandmother, from the doorway, holding a dish towel. "The porch gets one bar, the kitchen gets two. Come inside if it matters." She went back to her onions. Hannah carried the laptop to the kitchen table, where the light was better anyway, and looked at the last page again while her grandmother chopped.

The notes were all there, numbered correctly, sources intact. Nothing was missing. They were just in the wrong place, or possibly the right place, depending on a question Hannah now realized she had never actually considered: did the notes have to be on each page at all? She had a vague memory of Ms. Bear, her English teacher, saying something about a "standard citation style" and holding up a thick handbook, and Hannah had understood from this that there were rules, and that the rules were in a book she did not have, at a house twelve miles away.

She texted Thea. "do the notes have to be on the bottom of each page or can they all be at the end." Thea typed for a long time, long enough that Hannah ate half a biscuit. Then: "footnote = bottom of the page where you used it. endnote = same thing but collected at the end. both are real things people do. why."

Hannah read it twice. So what she had made, without meaning to, was the second thing, and the second thing was legitimate, a form that existed out in the world, that books used, that had a name. The word processor hadn't broken anything. It had made a choice for her, and the choice turned out to be allowed. She felt something loosen in her chest, though she was honest enough to admit that it didn't allay every worry: she still didn't know whether Ms. Bear wanted one form specifically, or whether "standard citation style" meant that either was fine as long as it was consistent. That part stayed uncertain. She could bring both views into her position on rankings, at least; on the notes, she could only pick and hope.

She spent an hour making everything uniform, checking the punctuation of the bibliography against the one example in her assignment sheet, which was itself possibly wrong. Ilan texted a photo of his own paper, all notes at the end, asking if that was the same disease hers had. "It's not a disease," she typed. "Yours are endnotes. They're allowed." He replied with a single thumbs up, which told her he had decided to trust her rather than find out for himself, and she decided not to hold it against him.

At six, her grandmother set down a bowl of stew and looked at the screen. "Finished?" It was a question about dinner as much as the paper. "Finished enough," Hannah said. She closed the laptop and wiped the table with the dish towel, both sides, the way she'd been taught. Outside the kitchen window the porch light came on, and somewhere down the road a dog began to bark at it, steadily, as though the light were something that had to be argued with until it went out.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The video arrived at 7:42 in the morning, while Addison was still holding her toothbrush, and by the time she reached her locker it had already been sent to her three more times. A warehouse on fire, a plume of black smoke, a caption in bold letters claiming the blaze had started the night before at a shipping plant two towns over, close enough that the wind might be carrying the ash toward the school. Anissa had forwarded it with no comment except a single exclamation mark, which for Anissa was practically a scream, and Asia had added, do your parents know?

Addison's thumb hovered over the forward button. Her mother worked nights at the hospital and slept through the morning; her father's shift at the plant had ended at six. If the smoke was drifting east, someone should wake them, warn them, and the fastest way to warn two hundred people was to press send. She had done it before, in seventh grade, with a photo of a flooded underpass that turned out, when the principal mentioned it at assembly, to be four years old and from another state. She still remembered the heat in her face when a boy named for a president nobody talked about anymore had said, you shared that fake thing, and she had said, everybody shared it, as though ubiquity were innocence.

She had ten minutes before first bell. She sat on the bench outside the computer lab, where the morning sun hit the concrete and the smell of floor wax drifted through the propped door, and she made herself stop. Not share, not decide, just stop. That much she remembered from a media literacy unit the year before, though the unit had mostly been Mr. Hernández telling them that headlines in all caps were usually trouble, advice so obvious it had slid off her.

What she had kept was a single term, and it came back to her now, unbidden, the way a song does: SIFT. She could even hear the student who had said it, a senior named Demarcus, during a class discussion about a fake evacuation order. "It's called SIFT," he had said, and then, "Stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace claims to their original context." Four moves, in that order, and Demarcus had demonstrated them in about ninety seconds on the projector while the class watched, some of them actually watching. Addison had watched. She had simply never needed it since, and need, she was discovering, was what converted a fact from trivia into a tool.

She carried her phone into the lab, where the radiators were already ticking with heat and a row of monitors glowed on idle screensavers. The account that posted the video had a name like a news outlet with one letter changed, a substitution so small it was almost elegant. She screenshotted a frame of the fire and dropped it into a reverse image search, and the results bloomed across the screen: the same smoke, the same collapsed roofline, dated three summers ago, in a country an ocean away. The local claim, the plant, the wind, the two towns over, all of it was embroidery stitched onto old cloth.

For a moment she felt the particular anger of someone who has been aimed at. Then something else, quieter: the memory of herself at thirteen, pressing forward on a flooded road because it felt like helping. Both impulses instantiated the same instinct, the urge to be the one who warns, and only one of them had been true. She could not fully separate them even now, sitting with proof on the screen. It might be, she thought, that the person who posted the video believed it, that they too had received it from a friend at some odd hour and had not checked. That was the unsettled part. Malice and happenstance could produce identical files, and no search result told you which you were looking at.

Anissa appeared in the doorway with her backpack on one shoulder and her phone out. "Did you see it? Half the freshmen think we're getting out early." Her voice had the bright panic of someone who wants the exciting thing to be real.

"It's from three years ago," Addison said. "Different country. I ran the image backward."

Anissa came closer and looked at the screen, at the duplicate smokestacks side by side. "So it's fake?"

"Old," Addison said. "The fire was real, just not here, not now." She was careful with the distinction, because it mattered and because she did not want to sound like a pamphlet. "Who sent it to you first?"

"Some guy from cross country." Anissa frowned at her phone. "I sent it to like ten people." Outside the lab window, a groundskeeper was dragging a hose across the soccer field, and the bell, when it rang, was closer than Addison had calculated; her embryonic plan of posting a correction to her whole grade before first period collapsed into something smaller. She could not chase down every copy of the video, and she understood, with a strange lightness, that she did not have to.

She typed a short reply to Anissa's thread instead: the fire is real but it's from 2021, in another country, here's the link, check before you resend. Then she found Asia in the hallway, near the trophy case, and showed her the two images, and Asia said, "Okay, that's embarrassing, I told my mom to check the air quality," and laughed, though not entirely.

Mr. Hernández was unlocking his classroom door two rooms down, and he glanced at the small crowd gathering around Addison's phone, but he said nothing, only raised an eyebrow and held the door. Whatever he knew or guessed, he was letting it belong to them. Addison walked in and took her seat near the window, where the sun had moved to the far edge of the sill, and she set her phone face down and listened to it buzz once, twice, with messages she had not read yet.

On her way to second period she passed a freshman holding up the burning warehouse to a friend, saying, my cousin says it's by the plant. Addison slowed, almost spoke, and kept walking, because she had one link and one class and no authority at all, and the choice of which fires to run toward was still, she suspected, something she would be learning for years. Behind her the freshman's voice carried down the hall, bright and certain, saying, "look at the smoke."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered grocery store had been empty since March, and Alexander had chosen it for exactly that reason: nothing to hit except light posts, and even those seemed forgiving. His grandmother was convalescing at home after her surgery, and his mother worked doubles at the hospital, which meant the drive to the physiotherapy clinic on Tuesday afternoons had landed on him, permit and all. The road test was scheduled for Friday. That left today, Thursday, one hour in an empty lot with Ms. Dang, the retired school secretary from across the street who still kept her instructor's certification current because, she said, she liked being useful.

Ms. Dang arrived in her own gray sedan and slid into the passenger seat with a thermos and a folder of laminated diagrams. Carter and Gurman came too, on bicycles, because Carter's own road test was next month and he wanted to watch for free what Ms. Dang charged forty dollars an hour to teach. Gurman came mostly, Alexander suspected, because there was nothing else to do in August, and because he had a theory that driving ability was largely phenotypic, some visible trait you either expressed or didn't, like height or the curl of your hair. He had been saying this since spring, and Alexander had never argued, though privately he felt it let people off the hook.

"Hands at nine and three," Ms. Dang said. "Not ten and two, whatever your uncle told you. We'll do a figure eight around those two posts, and then we'll talk about lanes."

The figure eight went badly, then less badly, then almost smoothly. Alexander felt the wheel begin to communicate something back to him, small resistances and invitations. Carter whooped from the curb. Gurman timed the laps on his phone and announced that Alexander's third was four seconds faster than his first, which was either improvement or luck, and Gurman declined to commit to either interpretation.

Then Ms. Dang had him drive the length of the lot as if it were a road, and imagine the painted line of a curb as a lane boundary, and practice moving over, as if to pass a slow car. He checked the mirror, signaled, and began to drift left.

"Stop," Ms. Dang said, not loudly, but her hand was already on the wheel. "Look again."

"There's nothing there," Alexander said. "I checked the mirror. Twice."

Gurman had quietly rolled his bike along the driver's side and stood beside the rear door, arms crossed, grinning, in a spot where the mirror showed nothing but empty asphalt and Alexander's own eyes, looking back at him from inside the car.

"Blind spot," Gurman said, tapping the window glass.

Ms. Dang nodded once. "A blind spot is the area around the car you can't see from your seat, even with the mirrors. Every car has them. That's why you turn your head before you change lanes, not just glance at the glass." She said it flatly, the way she'd once announced fire drills, and then she was quiet, letting him sit with it.

Alexander turned his head fully, chin past his shoulder, and there was Gurman, plain as a mailbox, standing exactly where he had been the whole time. The mirror had said empty. The mirror had lied, or rather the mirror had told only the truth it was built to tell. He thought of Gurman's phenotypic theory, that some people simply had the trait and some didn't, and understood suddenly that this was the theory's flaw: a trait you were born with couldn't be fixed by turning your head, and this could. It wasn't talent. It was a habit you either had or didn't, and a habit could be learned. Though he also admitted, sitting there with his neck craned and his signal still blinking, that knowing a thing and doing it under pressure on a real road with his grandmother's appointment time ticking toward him were different categories entirely, and Friday would test the second one whether he was ready or not.

They ran it again, and again. On the fourth pass, Alexander turned his head before the mirror check, then checked the mirror anyway, then moved over in one clean motion, and Ms. Dang made a small sound in her throat like a kettle deciding not to boil. On the fifth pass she said, "Good," which Carter later reported was, in Ms. Dang's currency, a fortune.

As the sun dropped behind the grocery store's roof, she checked her watch and began gathering her thermos. "One more," she said, "and then I have to get the casserole out of the oven before my son calls. He worries." She smiled at the word the way people smile at something both tiresome and dear. Alexander rolled slowly to the far end of the lot, signaled, glanced at the mirror, turned his head past his shoulder into the blind spot, found Gurman standing there yet again, and said, "Get out of my lane, you menace." Gurman stepped aside with a sweeping, ceremonial bow, and Alexander pulled forward through the empty spaces, hands steady at nine and three, the whole gray lot opening up in front of him.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Pencil 'lead' has never been made of the metal lead; the name comes from the 16th century, when graphite was mistaken for a kind of lead ore.
story:
The clock above the kiln read 1:47, and the district show pieces had to be on the loading dock by three. Nicole turned her slab of graphite in her hands, a block she had bought with her own money after deciding to abandon the watercolor she'd planned for a month. Alisha leaned over from the next table.

"You're not seriously starting over. With an hour."

"I'm not starting over. I'm starting."

Makena didn't look up from her canvas. She had been morose since lunch, since the list of accepted portfolios went up in the hallway and hers wasn't on it, and she was taking it out on a stretch of blue with a palette knife. "She's been like this since Tuesday," Makena said. "Bought a rock."

"It's not a rock." Nicole set the block down and picked up a burin she'd borrowed from the printmaking drawer. "It's graphite. You can draw with the whole thing, not just a sharpened point. That's the piece. The drawing is the pencil."

"That's the kind of thing a dilettante says," Alisha said. "You took one sculpture class freshman year."

Nicole didn't answer. Under the window, her phone buzzed: her mother, then her little cousin, then her mother again. She had the cousin that weekend, and he had chewed the end of a pencil through a whole math worksheet, and now her aunt was worried. She typed with one hand while she scored a line into the graphite's face.

The phone rang. She stepped into the hallway with it, burin still in her fist.

"I'm dying," her cousin said.
