"You're not dying."

"Aunt Rena says lead poison takes years to show up."

"Listen." She watched Ms. Malik wheel the drying rack past the doorway. "Pencil lead has never been made of the metal lead. It's graphite. The name is just from the 1500s, when people found graphite and thought it was a kind of lead ore. That's the whole thing. You chewed clay and graphite."

"So it's not poison."

"It's not poison. It's also why you can't get lead poisoning from a pencil, ever, so stop telling kids at school that."

He asked whether she was sure, and she said she was sure, and he asked what graphite was and she said she was holding a block of it right now, a big one, and she had to go. When she came back in, Alisha was reading the sketchbook Nicole had left open.

"You knew this already," Alisha said. "The graphite thing. That's why you dumped the watercolor."

Nicole took the sketchbook back. "Partly."

"Partly."

"The watercolor was for them." She nodded toward the acceptance list in the hallway, the direction of it. "Safe. A landscape everybody gets in the first second. This is me trying to say what a pencil actually is. Most people never think about it. They hold one every day and they think it's poison, or nothing."

Makena set the palette knife down. "So the kids who got in, they're the watercolors."

"I didn't say that."

"You thought it."

Nicole scored the graphite again, deeper, and a corner flaked off and she caught it in her palm. At 2:20 Ms. Malik came by, looked at the block, looked at the clock, and said only, "Loading dock, three o'clock, no exceptions for ambition."

She worked. The problem was the same one she'd been circling all week: she wanted the block to still look like a pencil, cylindrical, yellow, ordinary, and at the same time she wanted it cut open, the dark core exposed, the false name and the real substance in one object. Two ideas that fought each other. She had spent an hour trying to decide which one to give up, and somewhere in the second hour she had stopped trying to decide and started trying to build the argument between them. She didn't introspect well on demand; she thought with her hands, and the hands had begun to answer.

At 2:40 she had half a cylinder, the cut face raw silver-gray, the painted yellow skin peeled back like a label. It was ugly. It was also, she thought, honest, though she couldn't have defended that word against Alisha, who was watching from the next table with her finished, tidy, already-accepted-in-her-head watercolor.

"That's it?" Alisha said.

"That's it."

"It's not done."

"It's not done," Nicole agreed, and carried it toward the loading dock with ten minutes left, the burin still in her pocket, the flake of graphite in her palm like a coin she hadn't decided how to spend.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Any member of the US House of Representatives may introduce a bill in the House, and it is then referred to a committee for study.
story:
The letter from the congressman's office arrived on a Tuesday, folded into a cream envelope that felt more official than anything Alex had ever held. He read it twice at the kitchen table while his mother drained pasta behind him. "Thank you for your proposal regarding a pedestrian signal at the intersection of Marsh and Ninth," it said. "Please be advised that any member of the US House of Representatives may introduce a bill in the House, and it is then referred to a committee for study. Rep. Hale's office has forwarded your materials to our transportation legislative aide." Alex set the letter down and looked at the window for a long moment, at the orange of the streetlight coming on, because Anabel had crossed at Marsh and Ninth in October and the driver had not been speeding, only turning, only human.

He had written the email at one in the morning three weeks after it happened, after visiting her in the hospital where she kept apologizing for ruining his cross-country season, as if her leg were an inconvenience she had scheduled badly. He had found the address of the district office on his phone and typed four drafts. The one he sent was the shortest. He didn't expect an answer. He imagined the message dissolving into some federal vacuum, and instead here was a sentence that fit in his hand: any member may introduce a bill, and it is then referred to a committee. He said the word "referred" out loud, once, testing it.

But the letter also said, further down, that traffic signals on city streets were generally a municipal matter, and that if the city council took action, the office would be glad to support it. Alex had to look up "municipal." Then he had to look up when the council met. Thursday, seven o'clock, chambers on the fourth floor of the federal building, public comment period at the start.

He brought Rebeka because he didn't want to stand at the podium alone, and because she had been on the corner that day too, close enough to hear the sound the car made. They rode the bus downtown with his notes folded into his back pocket, and Rebeka kept asking him questions as if she were the one preparing. "So the congressman can't just do it?" "No," Alex said. "He can introduce a bill, but it goes to a committee first, and anyway this kind of thing starts here. With them." He nodded toward the building. It was the first time he had said the whole chain out loud, and saying it made it feel both real and flimsy, a promise made of paper.

The chambers were half full. A man proselytized about parking meters for eleven minutes until the mayor cleared her throat. A woman from the water department read a resolution about pipe replacement, and Alex watched the clerk pass copies down the dais, watched the council members read and initial them, and understood, suddenly, that this was drafting, that someone had sat with these clauses the way he had sat with his email. Ms. Ortiz, who taught civics at his school and also happened to sit on the council, looked up from her copy and found him in the audience. She didn't wave. She just marked something in the margin.

When the mayor called for public comment on non-agenda items, Alex's name sat second on the sign-in sheet. Walking to the podium, he lost his opening sentence entirely and began with the wrong one. "In October my friend was hit at Marsh and Ninth," he said. "I wrote to our congressman. His office wrote back that any member of the House may introduce a bill, but it goes to a committee, and it's the city's job anyway." He heard how clumsy it sounded, like a book report. Rebeka, from the third row, gave him a small nod. "So I'm here instead," he said, and then the rest came easier: the crossing count from the school's front office, the absence of a signal, the fact that the nearest crosswalk pushed students two blocks out of their way, which they would not walk, because teenagers are not ductile, they do not bend around bad design, they cross where they cross.

A council member with glasses asked whether the students would use a signal if one were installed, and Alex said some would and some wouldn't, and he did not pretend otherwise, because pretending had seemed, in the last month, like the thing that got people hurt. Ms. Ortiz asked him to submit his letter from the congressman's office for the record. He said yes. The mayor said the item would be referred to the public works committee for study, and Alex recognized the word, referred, the same word traveling a shorter distance.

Afterward, in the hallway by the water fountain, Rebeka said, "You sounded like you knew what you were doing." "I googled it on the bus," he said, and she laughed, and he laughed, and then neither of them laughed, because they both understood what the evening was actually about, and it wasn't procedure. Anabel had walked today for the first time without the boot, her mother had sent a photograph, and the photograph was the reason his voice had shaken at the count of the crossing, though he had kept his face still.

Ms. Ortiz caught up with them at the elevator. "Committee meets in three weeks," she said. "It can move slowly. Sometimes things die there." She said it without softening, which he respected more than comfort. "Sometimes they don't," she added.

The doors opened and the three of them stepped in, and Alex held Rebeka's binder while she pressed the button for the lobby, and the numbers above the door began their slow descent, four, three, two, ticking like something being counted.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: In 1904 physicist Robert W. Wood secretly removed a key prism from René Blondlot's apparatus, yet observers still reported seeing Blondlot's claimed 'N-rays', showing they were seeing what they expected.
story:
The physics of light exhibit was supposed to take twenty minutes, and Andrew's mother had dropped him off with the promise that the museum cafe would asuage any boredom with a lemon square afterward. He was only there because Ms. Nasser had offered extra credit, and he needed it, though he would not have admitted that to Mohamad, who was standing beside him with his hands in his pockets, reading the same wall text for the third time.

The trouble was the plaque. It described a French physicist named René Blondlot who, in 1903, claimed to have discovered a new kind of radiation, which he called N-rays. Dozens of other laboratories reported confirming the discovery. Then, in 1904, an American physicist named Robert W. Wood visited Blondlot's lab, and while the room was dark, he secretly removed a key prism from the apparatus. The observers went right on reporting that they saw the N-rays.

"He took the prism out," Andrew said. "Like, physically took it."

"Rude," said Mohamad, which was his word for anything genuinely unsettling.

What kept Andrew at the plaque was not the history. It was Friday afternoon in the school lab, two weeks ago, when his lab partner had stared at the interference pattern and said, "There, see it now? Right there." She had read the expected result in the manual first, and once she knew what to look for, the faint fringes had apparently arranged themselves obligingly. Andrew had seen almost nothing. He had let it go because he wanted to go, too, because the data table looked finished and the bell was coming.

"Did you see the fringes?" Mohamad asked now, as if he had been following the whole chain of thought, which sometimes he had.

"I said I did," Andrew said. "That's the thing. I said I did."

They walked on to a display case holding a replica of Blondlot's apparatus, brass and mahogany, with an empty slot where the prism would sit. A recorded voice played on a loop, a re-enactment of a lab assistant calling out the brightness of the rays, "stronger now, weaker now," while, according to the wall text, nothing in the room had changed at all. Mohamad listened to it with his head tilted, the way he listened to music he wasn't sure about yet.

"Imagine being Blondlot," he said. "Sixty years old. Famous. Everyone seeing your rays."

"He wasn't lying," Andrew said slowly. "That's what's bad about it. He believed it. They all did. Thirty papers, or however many, and it only took one guy with quiet hands." He was working it out as he said it, the shape of it: not one result, not even a hundred excited reports, but somebody willing to reach into the dark and take the thing away.

Ms. Nasser found them there, her lanyard swinging, holding two cups of water from the fountain because she had noticed Mohamad coughing on the bus and had not forgotten. She handed one over without comment. "The Wall of Retractions is around the corner," she said. "You two have been at this case longer than anyone today. Except a retired engineer who argued with me about determinism, saying the whole history of physics proves nothing is random. He was impervious to counterargument." She smiled and moved on toward a group of younger students, touching the shoulder of a boy who looked lost, steering him toward the optics room.

Andrew copied the plaque into his phone, the dates, the names, the word "replication," which appeared four times on the wall and which he had always thought of as a boring word, a word for the method section nobody read. Now it seemed closer to a kind of mercy. On Monday he would ask his lab partner to describe the fringes before she looked at the manual, and then after, and he would not tell her why, and he might still see nothing himself, and that would have to be written down too. He did not know if that would fix anything or just make the table messy.

"Come on," Mohamad said, draining his water and crushing the cup. "Lemon square. Then you're buying me a bus ticket to France so we can find Wood's descendants and shake their hands."

Andrew put his phone away. "Deal," he said, and followed him toward the cafe.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: In the seeding method, chopped chocolate that is already tempered is stirred into melted chocolate to supply form V crystals for the rest to copy.
story:
The thermometer clipped to Eliott's double boiler read forty-five degrees, and the chocolate behind it had gone liquid and amber at the edges, which was fine, and then the doorbell rang, which was not. Eliott's mother had called up the stairs that Mahmoud and the others were early, that they'd brought the cake already, that if the dipped strawberries were not on the table by seven Payton and Eliott would be dipping them in public like a pair of failed confectioners. Eliott wiped his hands on his jeans and said, "We have two hours and no marble slab."

Payton had spent the previous Saturday at the culinary annex downtown, where an instructor with steel-grey hair had demonstrated tempering on a slab of white marble, dragging melted chocolate across it with a palette knife until it thickened and shone. Payton had taken notes in a blue notebook, three pages of temperatures and motions, and had understood almost none of it. She understood dragging, and she understood shine, and she understood that between those two things lived a quantity of physics she could not yet contextualize within anything else she knew. It sat in her as an inchoate worry, a sense that success was a narrow door and she had the wrong key.

"Two hours," she said now, opening the notebook anyway. "We melt it to forty-five. Then we're supposed to cool it on marble to twenty-seven, then warm it back to thirty-one, and if it hits thirty-two we've ruined it."

"We don't have marble."

"You have a countertop."

"It's tile. It's warm tile. The sun hits it all afternoon." Eliott pressed his palm flat against it, and Payton pressed hers, and the tile gave back heat like a sleeping animal. She looked at the notebook page, at the arrow diagrams she'd drawn, and then she looked at the counter, and then at the bowl of chopped chocolate waiting beside the stove. Some of it came from a bar Eliott's mother had bought at the shop, glossy and hard and snapping in clean lines when Payton had broken it earlier. Some of it was the plain bulk chocolate from the market, dull, which they'd melted.

She picked up a shard of the shop bar and held it up to the window light. It gleamed. She snapped it beside her ear and heard the click of it, clean, like a knuckle.

"Wait," she said.

"What."

"This is already tempered. It's shiny, it snaps. The instructor kept saying the melted chocolate needs something to copy." She turned the shard over. "When she dragged it on the marble she kept saying she was making the right crystals form. But if the right crystals already exist in this bar, we could just stir them in. The chopped stuff that's already tempered gets stirred into the melted chocolate, and it supplies the crystals for the rest to copy. Like seeding a cloud."

Eliott frowned at her, then at the shard, then at the thermometer, which had begun to drift downward past forty-two. "Seeding," he repeated. "You're saying we skip the marble."

"I'm saying I think we skip the marble." She said it with the particular uncertainty of someone building a bridge over a gap she could not see the bottom of. The instructor had never mentioned this. The instructor had owned a marble slab the size of a door and had spoken of it the way sailors speak of hulls. But Payton had also watched a documentary clip on her phone two nights ago, half-asleep, in which a chocolatier in a small kitchen had done exactly what she was proposing, stirring chopped tempered chocolate into melted, and Payton had assumed she'd dreamt the convenient part.

They tried it. She stirred a small handful of the shards into the bowl off the heat, moving the spatula in slow figure eights, and the chocolate thickened by degrees, taking on a weight it hadn't had, a slow satin body. The thermometer passed thirty-two. She watched it like a hawk, reheating the bowl over the water for three seconds at a time, dragging it off again, until the reading settled at thirty-one. Eliott held out a metal spoon. She dipped it, swept the underside clean against the rim, and set it on the cool windowsill, and they both stood there doing nothing while it set, which was its own form of labour.

It took under four minutes. She touched the surface with a fingertip. It was hard, and when she flexed the spoon handle the coating split with a sound like a small dry branch. Under the window light it shone.

"Mahmoud's going to eat all of these before anyone else gets a plate," Eliott said, already hulling strawberries. Payton picked up the second spoon and dipped the first one, watching the chocolate sheet off in a glossy fall, and heard the front door open below them and Mahmoud's voice come up the stairwell asking about the smell.

"Up here," she called, and dipped another.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: 'Bottom Line Up Front', or BLUF, is a US military writing standard that puts the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details.
story:
The stockroom at Ferris Hardware smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and Levi had learned its rhythms well enough that he could restock washers by feel. What he had not learned was how to ask for something. On Thursday his manager, Ms. Zhao, had approved two extra weekend shifts for the older clerks and passed over him without a word, and when he'd caught her by the register she had said only, "Put it in writing," which was less an invitation than a door closing.

He drafted the email that night and hated it on sight. It began with an account of how long he'd worked there, moved through his mother's shifting hours at the hospital, mentioned the bike he'd bought for the commute, and arrived at the actual request, such as it was, somewhere in the fourth paragraph. It read like a bid for sympathy rather than a case, and he knew it, and he still pressed send at eleven because waiting felt worse.

No reply came Friday. On Saturday Gracelyn clocked in beside him, read the email over his shoulder when he opened it on the break-room phone, and winced. "It's all background," she said. "By the time she finds out you want the Sunday shift, she's already annoyed."

"Shawn says the army solved this." He'd heard it from Shawn the night before, in the parking lot, half-shouted over the truck's idling engine. Shawn's older brother was at basic training and sent home letters like memos. "Shawn calls it BLUF," Levi said. "Bottom Line Up Front. It's a US military writing standard. The main point or the request goes in the first lines, before any of the supporting details."

Gracelyn scrolled back to the top of his draft. "So lead with the ask."

"Then the reasons after. If she wants them."

It sounded simple, and it was not. Levi sat on an overturned milk crate between shelves of galvanized nails and rewrote the message in his head all morning, because rewriting it on the stockroom terminal meant Ms. Zhao might glance up from her desk and see him composing what was, in effect, a complaint about her decision. The first attempt was blunt to the point of rudeness, two lines that read like an ultimatum. The second drifted back into apology. Somewhere between the two, he began to understand that form was not decoration. The shape of the message was itself a message. A rambling email said, I am uncertain and I hope you will be charitable. A front-loaded one said, I know what I want and I respect your time enough to say it first.

There was also the matter of what he was actually asking for, which he had been dodging. He didn't want the shifts purely for the money, though the money mattered; he had half-convinced himself he was requesting them for some altruistic reason, coverage for the store, relief for the exhausted weekend crew. That was partly true and partly a costume. He wanted his name on the schedule before the older clerks' idiosyncrasies ossified into permanent fact, before the way things had been done in August became the way they would be done forever. Naming that honestly, to himself and to her, was harder than any of the sentence work.

He typed the rewrite during his lunch, on the register terminal turned slightly toward the window.

"Ms. Zhao," it began. "Request: reassignment to the Sunday inventory shift currently given to second-year clerks, effective next schedule. Reason: I have completed the scanner training and my weekday availability has changed due to a family schedule conflict, which I can document. Happy to discuss before the schedule posts if the assignment is fixed."

He read it four times. It was colder than anything he would say out loud, and colder felt dangerous, like a tone that could be mistaken for a challenge. But it also didn't hide behind the bike or the hospital or the washers he'd restocked, and some stubborn part of him insisted that this was the fairer thing to offer her. He sent it before he could sand the edges off.

She found him at three, by the paint mixer. "Your email," she said. "You went from a page and a half to six sentences."

"It was too much before."

"It was." She watched the shaker rattle. "The scanner training, did you actually finish it?"

"Certificate's in my folder. Shawn supervised the last module."

"Shawn signs off on things for everybody. That's a separate conversation." She took a can of primer from the shelf and turned it in her hands, checking the tint ring. "The Sunday shift isn't a promotion, Levi. It's four hours of counting in a cold room."

"I know what it is."

She set the can down. "Here's my problem with the first email, since you're being direct now. It asked me to feel something. The second one asks me to decide something. Those aren't the same request, and people send the first when they're afraid of the second."

He hadn't thought of it that way, and he didn't fully accept it either, because the reasons in the first email were real, not inventions; the bike and the bus route were facts of his life, and a request stripped of them was a thinner kind of honest. But he could see that the six sentences had given her something she could act on, and the page and a half had given her something she could only file.

"I still want the shift," he said.

"Then you'll take it from the fourth of next month, not sooner, and you'll do the counting module first so I'm not sending you in blind." She picked up her clipboard. "And the documentation you mentioned. Bring it Monday, one page."

He waited until she was halfway down the aisle, then let out a breath he'd been holding since the register. He pulled his phone from his apron pocket and typed to Shawn: it worked. Under the shelf labels, half a dozen screws had rolled into the wrong bin sometime that morning, and he knelt and sorted them back one by one, gold to gold, steel to steel.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
Keira had taped the graph above her desk so that when she woke it was the first thing she saw: a thin red line climbing in small, patient steps, then steepening after 1950 like a road deciding to become a mountain. Carbon dioxide, parts per million, one hundred years. She had chosen it for her presentation in Ms. Kamau's environmental science class because it looked simple, and she was beginning to suspect it was not.

The problem was the essay that came with it. Ms. Kamau wanted them to explain, in their own words, how greenhouse gases trapped heat, and then take a position on a policy question. Keira had picked what seemed like the obvious one: whether cutting methane leaks should come first. Her father worked at the utility company, and he had mentioned, over dinner, that they were replacing old pipes. That was the thread. She had pulled it and found a tangle.

She met Cierra by the vending machines before first period, both of them waiting for the machine to decide whether it believed in dollar bills. "Your thing is on methane, right?" Cierra said. "Dax was arguing about it yesterday. He says carbon dioxide is the only thing that matters because there's so much more of it."

"There is more of it," Keira said. The machine returned her dollar, creased and offended. "But that's not the whole story. I read this thing last night and I can't stop thinking about it."

"Tell me at lunch."

She told her at lunch, on the bench near the fence where the wind came through, pulling her notebook from her bag. "Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide," she said. "Like, way more. But a methane molecule only stays in the atmosphere for about a decade on average. Carbon dioxide stays much longer."

"So it's stronger but shorter," Cierra said, unwrapping her sandwich.

"Stronger but shorter, weaker but basically forever." Keira looked at her own page, where she had written both phrases and underlined neither. "So if you want to slow warming in the next few years, cutting methane leaks would do it faster. But if you want to fix the long run, the carbon dioxide is what stays." She paused. "I think. I'm not sure which one I'm supposed to think is more important."

"That's the fun part," Cierra said. "You're allowed to not be sure."

Keira was not sure she believed that. School had a way of rewarding certainty, the essay that landed on one side and stayed there, and she had habituated herself to writing that way, the confident topic sentence, the tidy conclusion. She had gotten good grades by deciding things early. Now she sat in the library during study hall with two browser tabs open, one about pipe replacement and one about the graph, and felt her old method failing her. The graph told one story, slow and cumulative, a century of accumulation. The methane fact told another, quick and sharp, a decade of consequence. Both were true. She kept trying to make one of them false.

Dax found her there and dropped into the chair across from her, chin on his fist. "Cierra says you're doing methane. I still say it's a distraction. Carbon dioxide is eighty percent of the problem. Why would you fix the small thing first?"

"Because of how fast it works," Keira said. "Cut the leaks and the effect shows up in years, not decades. The molecules that are already up there go away on their own in about ten years. Carbon dioxide doesn't. It stays for centuries. So the stuff we emitted at your parents' wedding is still up there working." Dax frowned, and she watched the frown change shape as he turned it over, the first loosening of someone who had been holding a position like a door held shut against wind. "But here's what I keep getting stuck on. If we cut methane and not carbon dioxide, we get a reprieve. Ten years, maybe a little more, of slightly slower warming. And then what? The carbon dioxide we kept emitting the whole time is still there. The mountain keeps growing."

"So methane first is like paying the interest on a loan," Dax said slowly, "and carbon dioxide is the loan."

Keira laughed, surprised. "That's better than anything in my draft." She looked at the screen, at the red line climbing its patient steps, and something shifted in her, small and inchoate, a way of holding two ideas at once instead of racing to drop one. Maybe the answer was both, in order. Maybe the answer was that ordering was the whole argument. She wrote that down, then crossed out crossed it out, then wrote it again.

On Friday she stood at the front of Ms. Kamau's class with the graph projected behind her, and explained the greenhouse effect the way she had finally come to understand it, as a matter of molecules absorbing outgoing heat and reradiating it, some fraction returning downward, the atmosphere thickening its blanket molecule by molecule. Then she gave her position: cut methane leaks first for the near term, treat it as the decade's brake, while the harder, slower work on carbon dioxide went on underneath it, because a molecule of carbon dioxide, once emitted, lingered far beyond any human planning horizon, and a molecule of methane, on average, did not. She said she was certain about the physics and uncertain about the priority, and that the uncertainty seemed to her like the honest place to stand.

Afterward Ms. Kamau asked whether she had considered that the graph itself might change how a reader felt about methane, and Keira said she hadn't, not until that second, and stood a moment with her notes still in her hand, thinking about what a hundred years of red line does to the eye, how it trains the eye to distrust anything short.

She was still thinking about it at her locker when Dax appeared beside her, holding his phone. "So I changed my mind," he said. "Methane matters. I'll give you that." He tapped the screen. "But I found this article about a proposed pipeline through the wetlands, and I want to write the counter-argument to your presentation for the class debate. Someone should argue the other side properly. Someone should stress-test it." He grinned. "And I want to win."

Keira closed her locker and shouldered her bag. "You want to lose an argument you just agreed with?"

"I want to find out if it survives me," Dax said, and held out his phone so she could see the graph on it, her red line, already climbing.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, some Soviet archives became available to researchers, giving historians evidence about Stalin's decisions that earlier writers never had.
story:
Oliver had been sent to his grandfather's house for the weekend on the theory that fresh air would improve his history essay, and so far the fresh air had improved nothing but his appetite. The essay was due Monday. The question was cruel in its simplicity: two historians, one arguing that the Cold War grew out of Soviet expansion driven by ideology, the other that it grew out of mutual fear and Western provocation, and which explanation did the evidence better support? Oliver had read both chapters twice on the train and now understood each writer's position perfectly and had no idea whatsoever what he himself thought.

He found the books in his grandfather's study, which smelled of pipe tobacco and old paper, two entire shelves of Cold War histories with dates penciled inside the covers. His grandfather had been a schoolteacher once and had evidently prognosticated, back in the sixties, that this subject would keep producing arguments for decades, because the collection ran from a fat volume published in 1963 to a slim, angry-looking paperback from 1998. Oliver pulled out the two extremes and carried them to the kitchen, where his grandfather was doing something mysterious to a radiator with a spanner.

"Grandad, did you ever argue about this stuff?"

"With your grandmother, mostly about whether I'd bought too many books about it. She held that fifty was too many. I held that fifty was a floor, not a ceiling." He wiggled the spanner. The radiator clanked its agreement. "Why, what's the puzzle?"

Oliver explained the two historians, and his grandfather listened with the particular stillness of a man delighted to be consulted. "Well," he said, "you could do what I did with my classes. Read the old one first and pretend you don't know how it comes out. Then read the new one and work out what changed. But mind, I'm not telling you the answer. That's cheating, and also I want my radiator done."

The 1963 book was confident in the way only people writing very close to events can be. Stalin, its author insisted, was malevolent by design and expansionist by doctrine, and the West had merely reacted. There were no documents to check, so the prose had to do all the work, and it did it with style, sweeping and certain and, Oliver noticed, slightly sweaty. He texted Brielle a photo of the most emphatic paragraph. "This guy has never once said 'probably,'" he wrote. She replied with a picture of her own essay, which was two lines long, one of which said "probably." Brenden, added to the group without asking, sent a single question mark, which Oliver felt was Brenden's most honest contribution to any conversation all year.

The 1998 book was different. Its author used the same word, "malevolent," about Stalin, but then did something the earlier writer hadn't: he kept quoting things. Notes from meetings. Telegrams. A memo Stalin had actually read, with what it said printed right there on the page. Oliver sat forward. He checked the citations, then checked them again, then flipped to the front of the book and found a short paragraph thanking several archives in Moscow. He read it four times. Somewhere between the third and fourth reading, the whole shape of his essay rearranged itself in his head like the radiator pipes when his grandfather finally gave the valve a decisive turn.

He called Brielle, who answered eating something crunchy. "Okay, so the sixties guy couldn't know what Stalin was deciding, because the stuff was locked up. But after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, some of the Soviet archives opened up. Researchers could get in. The nineties guy was reading the actual papers." He was talking too fast and didn't care. "So when he says Stalin's decisions were driven by security panic and not some master plan, he's not just being stylish about it. He's got the memos."

"Wait," Brielle said, "so the newer one wins? Essay done, come eat dinner."

But Oliver, lying on the carpet of the study with the two books open on his chest, wasn't sure it was that clean. The archives proved what Stalin had decided, not why he had decided it, and fear could be an amalgam of real insecurity and genuine cruelty, both at once, the way his grandfather's radiator was partly fixed and partly a threat. Maybe the sixties writer's certainties were wrong but his instincts weren't entirely. Oliver wrote that down, then crossed it out, then wrote it again in the margin where he couldn't lose it.

At dinner he told his grandfather all of it, the memos, the open archives, the part he still couldn't settle. His grandfather nodded slowly and pushed the potatoes toward him.

"So which is it, then?" Oliver asked. "Fear or expansion?"

"That's not for me to prognosticate," his grandfather said, and spooned himself a second helping. "But I'll say this: you argued with two dead men all afternoon and both of them got a word in. That's more than your grandmother ever let me manage."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
Nolan arrived at his grandmother's house on December 26 carrying a shoebox of candles he'd been sent to buy, and the first thing his aunt said to him at the door was, "You're doing Umoja tonight."

He had assumed he would eat, hand his grandmother her gift, and sit near the back with his phone. Instead he stood in the hallway holding the box while coats were piled on his arms, and the assignment settled on him the way chores did in this house, without negotiation. The kinara was already on the mantel, seven spaces, one black candle in the center with three red to its left and three green to its right, none of them lit yet.

"I don't actually know what to say," he told his cousin Leanne in the kitchen, where she was folding napkins into fans with more precision than the job required. She was fifteen and treated every family gathering like a performance she had rehearsed for.

"That's why you say yes," she said. "You learn it, then you say it. Grandmother asked you, not me, so." She refolded a napkin that had been fine.

His friend Dani had come along because her own family was scattered across three states this year and she had said, casually, that she'd never been to a Kwanzaa celebration, only read about it in a unit at school that circumscribed the whole thing to a single handout. Now she stood in the kitchen doorway with a cup of cider, and Nolan felt the evening divide in two: the part where he was a grandson, and the part where he was someone's tour guide.

"Okay, so what is it actually?" Dani asked. "All I know is candles."

Nolan started to say he'd look it up, then remembered his grandmother had no patience for phones at the table. He went to the living room instead, where his grandfather's old books were shelved below the family photographs, and found a thin paperback his grandmother had bought decades ago, its spine cracked white. Maulana Karenga had created Kwanzaa in 1966, the first pages said, and the celebration ran from December 26 to January 1, seven days for seven principles, one each day, beginning tonight with Umoja. He read the word three times before he trusted his pronunciation.

At dinner, between the collards and the sweet potato pie, the table got loud in the good way, everyone talking across each other, his uncle retelling a story everyone could recite along with. Dani sat beside Nolan and asked quiet, real questions, and he watched his grandmother soften toward her, adding food to Dani's plate before Dani asked for it, which in this house was the highest compliment available.

Then the plates were cleared, and his grandmother lit the black candle, and the room went quiet in a way that felt older than the house. "Nolan," she said. "Umoja."

He stood up. He had a maxim prepared, something he'd copied from the book about striving for and maintaining unity in family, community, nation, race, and it had sounded noble on the page. Said aloud, it sounded borrowed. He looked at Leanne, who gave him a small nod like a coach sending in a play, and he looked at Dani, who was watching him with her whole attention, and he put the paper in his pocket.

"Umoja means unity," he said. "That's the first principle, the first day." His voice steadied as he went on. He said he'd been reading about it only an hour before, that he hadn't known Karenga's name or that the holiday was only as old as his parents, that part of him had thought the whole thing felt anachronistic, a ritual performed for a past nobody in the room had lived. He heard his grandmother's breath change and kept going anyway. "But it's not trying to be the past. It's seven days, one at a time, starting with us at one table. And we're at one table." He stopped there, because the next sentence he'd planned was a summary, and it didn't feel true.

His uncle broke the silence by saying, "That's more than your father ever said, and he had the paper." Laughter moved down the table. Leanne, folding napkin fans in her lap even now, mouthed, "Told you."

Afterward, in the kitchen, his grandmother found him drying the pie pan. "You threw away what you wrote," she said. It wasn't a question, and it wasn't a complaint, though he couldn't tell which it was closer to.

"It wasn't mine," he said. "I mean, it was true, but it wasn't something I'd figured out yet."

She took the dish towel from him and folded it, once, precisely. "Tomorrow is Kujichagulia," she said. "Self-determination. You'll figure that one out standing up too." She carried the towel toward the laundry, then paused at the doorway. "Your friend asked me for the recipe. I wrote it on the back of the invitation." Through the kitchen door, Nolan could see Dani at the living room mantel, holding the unlit red candle from the second night, turning it slowly in her fingers like she was memorizing its weight.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Niger has one of the highest birth rates in the world, so its population pyramid has a very wide base and a large share of children.
story:
The departure board kept flipping between DELAYED and ON TIME, as if it could not make up its mind either. Landon sat with his back against a pillar in Concourse C, the school trip to St. Louis now postponed by two hours, and Ms. Pierre had done the thing she always did at moments like this: she had handed out an assignment. Each of them got a printed sheet with two population pyramids, side by side, and the instruction to say which country needed more schools and which needed more nursing homes, and to be ready to defend the answer on the plane.

Madalyn had already claimed the only outlet within thirty feet, her charger plugged in beside a family eating hamburgers, and she was working with the flattened concentration of someone who intended to be finished before boarding. "Japan's the easy one," she said without looking up. "It's shaped like a light bulb. Old on top, skinny at the bottom. Nursing homes, obviously." She tapped the second sheet. "This one I don't get. It's basically a triangle."

Landon looked at the triangle. It was labelled Niger, though he had only found that out by turning the sheet over, where Ms. Pierre had written the countries in small pencil letters, presumably to make them work for it. The pyramid was wide at the bottom, wide almost past belief, each bar for the youngest age groups jutting out farther than the one above it. It narrowed fast, so that by the middle it was thin, and near the top, where the ages climbed past seventy-five, there was barely anything at all. He counted the bars with his finger. Half the picture, or close to it, was children.

"Move over," said Marvin, dropping onto the bench beside him with a paper cup of coffee the size of a thermos. "I paid seven fifty for this, which is profligate, I know, but I refuse to be awake and miserable when I can be awake and merely broke." Marvin's plan for the trip, announced on the bus to the airport, was a schedule of pure hedonism: sleep on the plane, buy nothing in Missouri except food, and see the arch from the hotel window without leaving the bed. He had, so far, spent the delay trying to find a seat near a power outlet, and Madalyn's was the last one, and she was not moving.

"That's not a light bulb," Landon said, tilting Madalyn's Japan sheet next to his own. Hers bulged in the middle and narrowed at the base, like a top-heavy tree. His narrowed toward the sky, steep on both sides, a triangle with its point clipped off. He set them side by side on the bench, and Marvin, glancing down with his cup halfway to his mouth, said, "Why does yours look like a slide? Where'd everybody go?"

"They didn't go anywhere. They're all at the bottom." Landon traced the lowest bar. "Look how wide this is. Zero to four years old. That's more people than any other bar, by a lot." He worked upward, and it was like watching a crowd thin out in reverse, the way a school hallway thins as the little kids give way to the tall ones. If half the bars near the bottom were children, then the country was mostly children. He thought of his own elementary school, four wings of it, and how the town had closed one wing the year after his class moved on. A place shaped like Japan would be closing wings. A place shaped like Niger would be building them, and hiring teachers, and pouring foundations.

"So it's schools," Madalyn said, still not looking up, but her pen had stopped moving, which meant she was listening. "Fine. But Ms. Pierre said defend the answer. How do you prove a country needs schools from a picture?"

"You have to operationalize it," Landon said. He had picked the word up from a documentary his father watched about city planning, and it had stuck. "Turn the shape into something countable. If the wide part is the bottom half, then you're counting how many kids there are per classroom that exists. The picture tells you the kids. The need is the difference." He was not entirely sure that was a defensible answer, and he said so. "It might also need both. A triangle can still have old people at the top. Just not many. I'd say mostly schools, and I'd say I can't be sure about the rest."

Madalyn wrote one sentence, crossed it out, and wrote another. Marvin had drifted toward the window, where a baggage train was crossing the tarmac in the slow, ceremonial way of things that are never late because nothing waits for them. The coffee was gone. He looked at Madalyn's outlet, then at the family still eating, then at the sky, which had begun to let down a thin rain.

Ms. Pierre came back from the gate with a boarding time, and Landon held up his sheet. "Niger is schools," he said. "Mostly."

"Mostly is a real word in geography," she said, and kept walking.

Marvin leaned over Madalyn's shoulder and pointed at the empty outlet, and Madalyn, without a word, slid her charger out and offered him the plug.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
Makayla had been free of symptoms for six days, which meant that on Monday morning she stood at the shallow end of the pool with a kickboard and permission to do light drills, the first real work since the door of the Honda Civic had met her forehead in the school parking lot three weeks ago. Mr. Demetriou held a laminated sheet in one hand and a stopwatch in the other. Step four, the sheet said. She had memorized the sheet by now, mostly out of boredom during step one, which had been total rest, no screens, no reading, nothing but lying on the couch listening to her mother describe the genealogy of the neighbor's divorce in exhausting detail.

"The whole thing goes rest, then light activity, then sport-specific stuff without risk, then full contact practice, then the meet," Coraly said, treading water beside her. Coraly had done the protocol last season after clipping her head on the starting block, so she spoke about it the way people speak about a bus route they ride every day. "You only move up if you stay free of symptoms. Headache comes back, you go down a step."

"That's the rule," Makayla said. "I've read it forty times."

"Reading it and doing it are different animals."

The humor, such as it was, had become a team habit. At the dryland session on Tuesday, Zac held up a foam roller and announced that his role on the team was now vestigial, like an appendix, since Makayla was back and his job as her designated bag carrier was over. She had made him carry her bag for two weeks because looking down at the floor made the pool lights buzz behind her eyes. He had accepted the role with a gravity that suggested knighthood.

The season had one meet left, the conference final, and Makayla wanted the hundred fly more than she had wanted anything since she'd learned to swim. She was honest with herself about the arithmetic: she had missed three weeks of water, her feel for the stroke was gone, and the team's medley relay needed her split. Mr. Demetriou had not mentioned the relay. He mentioned it on Thursday, after practice, while she toweled her hair by the chain-link gate.

"You'd anchor," he said. "If you clear step five by Saturday."

"I'll clear it."

"Full practice, no symptoms. That's what clearing it means."

She thought about the sheet again that night, and about something Coraly had said in the fall, back when Coraly herself was on step three and Makayla, healthy and impatient, had thought the whole protocol was bureaucratic caution dressed up as science. She had actually said that out loud, in the bleachers, that it problematized nothing, it just slowed people down. Coraly had looked at her for a long moment and said, "It's not there to be interesting. It's there because brains don't get do-overs." Makayla had changed the subject to the pasta fundraiser. She remembered that now with the specific discomfort of recalling your own confident stupidity.

Friday's practice was the full one, and it went wrong for Coraly, not for her. Twenty minutes into the light drill set, a set Coraly had been cleared for after her own collision with the backstroke flags, Coraly stopped mid-lane and hung on the rope. "It's back," she said, flat. "The headache. Same one." Mr. Demetriou pulled her out, and Makayla watched from the next lane as he explained, quietly, that she'd go back a stage and rebuild from there. Coraly nodded, jaw tight, and swam a slow, easy lap to the ladder, which was the form the protocol's lower step took: light movement, no strain, symptoms watched like weather.

Makayla finished the set. Her head stayed quiet. At the end, Mr. Demetriou wrote something on his laminated sheet and showed it to her: step five, Saturday, full practice, and then, in smaller letters, the meet. She stood at the gutter, breathing hard, and found that her certainty about the relay had gone strange and thin. She wanted it, and she believed she was ready, and she also understood, for the first time from the inside, that those were two different claims and only one of them was hers to make. Saturday would decide the second one regardless of the first.

She walked to Coraly's lane before leaving. Coraly was sitting on the deck with her cap in her lap.

"Tomorrow," Makayla said.

"Tomorrow," Coraly said. "Kick once for me."

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Winston Churchill said in a speech at Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946, that an iron curtain had descended across Europe.
story:
Thomas had promised Ms. Quinn the books back by four, and it was already quarter past three, which meant he had forty-five minutes to decide whether the Cold War had been caused by fear or by ambition, and no idea how to begin.

He spread the two histories on the carrel table like opposing hands of cards. One argued that the United States and the Soviet Union had stumbled into hostility, two exhausted powers misreading each other's intentions until the misreadings hardened into policy. The other argued the opposite, that Soviet expansion was deliberate and that the West's response, however clumsy, had been necessary. Shaan, who had read the first book in one sitting, leaned over from the next carrel.

"That one's obviously right," Shaan said. "Nobody wants a war. They were both scared."

"Wanting and being scared aren't the only options," Thomas said, and immediately regretted it, because Shaan grinned the way he did before an argument that would eat the whole period.

Justine arrived with her own book held open against her hip, having underlined so much that some pages had gone mostly yellow. She sat down without being asked. "My historian says the Americans were canny, not frightened. They knew exactly what they were doing with the Marshall Plan. Canny people don't stumble."

"That's the same word my dad uses for people he doesn't trust," Shaan said.

"That's because it means people who are too clever to be innocent."

Ms. Quinn passed behind them with a cart of returns and paused at the pile on the table. She picked up the first history, read the back cover, and set it down again with the gentle finality of someone returning a chess piece. "The essay asks you to weigh the explanations against the evidence," she said. "Not to pick a side by Monday. Evidence first." She rolled the cart toward the history shelves, and Thomas watched her go, half grateful and half annoyed, because evidence was exactly the thing he didn't have. Both books made claims. Neither showed him how to test them.

He pulled the document collection from the bottom of the pile, the one Ms. Quinn had left on the reserve shelf with a sticky note in her slanted handwriting. He turned to 1946 and started reading, and there it was, dated March 5, in a place called Fulton, Missouri, and he read it twice before saying it out loud.

"'From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.'"

Justine looked up. "That's Churchill? I thought that was later. Like a slogan that developed over time."

"It's a speech," Thomas said. "Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946." He said the date slowly, the way you say a phone number you're trying to keep. "So a year after the war ends, he's already calling it a curtain. A curtain you can't see through."

Shaan came around the table and read over his shoulder. "Okay, but a curtain isn't a wall. He's not saying nobody can cross it. He's saying nobody can see past it." Shaan tapped the page. "That actually helps my guy. If the West couldn't see what Stalin wanted, then fear makes sense. The curtain underpins the misreading, not the aggression."

Thomas wrote it down before he could lose it. Then he sat with his pen stopped, because the same words could be bent the other way, and he knew it, and Justine knew it too, because she was already talking.

"Or a man who thought it was a wall chose curtain on purpose," she said. "Churchill wanted the Americans alarmed. A curtain sounds defensive. A wall sounds like an accusation." She flipped through her historian's chapter on 1946 and found almost nothing on Fulton, which Thomas noticed and she noticed him noticing.

"So your book doesn't deal with it," he said.

"My book deals with economics. It doesn't have to deal with every speech."

"It's the most famous sentence anyone said that year."

They looked at each other across the table, and Thomas understood that the moment had a fork in it. He could push, and win, and Shaan would laugh, and Justine would close her book with that particular softness she used instead of slamming things. Or he could say what was actually true, which was less useful and harder.

"I don't know what the speech proves," he said. "I know when it was said and where. I know what it claimed. Whether Churchill believed it or performed it, whether Stalin meant what Churchill said he meant, the documents in this pile don't say. My guy assumes the fear was sincere. Your guy assumes it was theater. Both of them skip the part where it's undecidable from here."

"That's going to be a terrible essay," Shaan said.

"It's going to be an honest one."

Justine uncapped her pen. "Then I'll write the paragraph where mine explains the speech my book skipped. If I'm wrong, you can say so in the margin."

The clock over the circulation desk read 3:58. Thomas began gathering the books, stacking them with the spines aligned out of habit, and under the document collection he found the sticky note Ms. Quinn had left, which he had never actually read. On it she had written a single line: "Evidence is rarely on anyone's side." He folded it in half and put it in his pocket, then carried the pile to the desk, where Ms. Quinn was waiting with the date stamp already in her hand.
